news.title: Trump Says He'd Beat Obama 'Easily' in Potential Presidential Race
news.text: President Donald Trump said that he could "easily" beat former President Barack Obama in a hypothetical matchup, while calling his predecessor "highly overrated." In a sit-down with Stephen A. Smith on Smith's podcast Straight Shooter on Thursday, Trump said, "I got many more votes than he got. And I got many more votes in the states...I have most of the state records of the big states. If you take a look at Texas, I have the all-time record, Florida I have the all-time record." Smith then asked Trump if he was implying that he'd beat Obama, "Yeah, I think I'd beat him easily, yeah. I think he's highly overrated." In the 2024 presidential election, Trump won all the swing states and the popular vote with 77,304,290 votes compared to Vice President Kamala Harris' 75,019,761 votes. In the 2012 election, Obama defeated Republican Mitt Romney with 62,611,250 votes compared to 59,134,475 votes. Trump's remarks to Smith come on the heels of sweeping midterm losses for the Republican Party that saw House and Senate majority flip in favor of the Democrats. The president conceded partially that the landslide Democratic wins could be due to the war in Iran, although he said he would still do it again. Similarly, Democrats lost the midterms in 2010 while Obama was in office. Newsweek reached out to the office of Barack and Michelle Obama via online portal Thursday night for comment. What To Know In his comments to Smith about Obama, Trump added, "I just think, that's just my opinion, I think he's overrated. I didn't think he was a good president, I thought he was a divider." Smith then asked Trump how he'd classify himself, which he answered, "as a person that brings people together." In the 2024 presidential election cycle, Trump obtained 6,110,125 votes in Florida versus 4,683,038 votes for Harris, according to the Florida Department of State Division of Elections. In 2012, Obama obtained 4,237,756 votes in the Sunshine State and Romney landed 4,163,447 votes. In state voting data reviewed by Newsweek dating over 40 years, Trump had the most votes for a presidential nominee in Florida. In Texas, Trump obtained 6,393,597 votes compared to Harris' 4,835,250 votes in the 2024 presidential election. In 2012, Obama had 3,294,440 votes in the Lone Star State compared to Romney's 4,555,799 votes. Newsweek also reviewed state voting data going back decades in Texas, and Trump had the most votes out of any presidential nominee. Texas has been known as a Republican stronghold for presidential elections, and Florida has shifted to the right over time and is now also seen as a reliable pickup for GOP presidential candidates. Robert Collins, professor of public policy at Dillard University, told Newsweek on Thursday: "This is clearly just President Trump throwing red meat to his base. Given the president currently has a national job approval rating in the 30s, no rational observer believes he could beat Obama in a head-to-head matchup right now. "His past remarks on the possibility of running for a third term are also just trying to keep his base happy. No serious constitutional scholar believes there is any legal way for President Trump to run for a third term." The president's interview with Smith also touched on Iran, working with Democrats during the remainder of his term, gasoline prices, immigration policy and his legacy. Trump and Obama's Popularity & Approval Compared In a CNN-SSRS poll conducted earlier this year, 57 percent said they had a favorable opinion of Obama versus 32 percent who had an unfavorable opinion. Comparatively, Trump had a 34 percent favorability rating versus a 55 percent unfavorable rating. When asked which president they admire the most, Obama landed 30 percent and Trump had 19 percent, the poll shows. The poll was conducted from May 7 to May 31 among 2,480 respondents and had a margin of error of 2.7 percent. In a YouGov/Economist poll this week, Trump's approval rating is 32 percent versus a 63 percent disapproval rating. The poll surveyed 1,685 U.S. citizens from November 9 to November 11 and had a margin of error of 3 percent. In a November 2010 poll after the midterm elections, Obama's approval was 42 percent with a 49 percent disapproval rating, also in a YouGov/Economist poll. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: In a sit down with Stephen A. Smith, Trump took repeated swipes at Obama, while saying he could beat him in a hypothetical race.
news.author: Anna Commander

news.title: Gavin Newsom reveals his timeline for deciding 2028 presidential run
news.text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom said he will decide by early January whether to run for president in 2028, revealing his political timetable during a trip to the COP31 international climate conference in Turkey where he delivered criticism of President Trump.

“I’ll make the determination at the beginning of the year, so we’ll spend the next few weeks with the family and make a decision early January,” Newsom told Turkey’s Anadolu news agency, calling the midterm elections a “rebuke” of Trump. 

Newsom’s remarks elevate yet another international trip in which he praised California’s environmental policies and attacked Trump’s retreat from global climate pacts.

The outgoing governor met with Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to discuss expanding California’s climate partnership with Brazil, and he finalized a new climate agreement with Portugal, according to the governor’s office.

The governor and his wife Jennifer Siebel Newsom also visited a forestry training center to exchange wildfire lessons, and he joined governors and mayors — including Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz and London Mayor Sadiq Khan — at a gathering convened by U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres.

Newsom’s international globetrotting this year has generally been paid for by wealthy benefactors who fund the California State Protocol Foundation, a nonprofit that has paid for Newsom’s travel expenses instead of taxpayer money.

Newsom and his wife are currently the focus of federal investigations, and feds reportedly requested information about the Protocol Foundation’s donors and fundraisers in subpoenas. Investigators were seeking the governor’s international travel and events, and any money used for the governor’s living and personal expenses, according to the San Francisco Standard.

But new polling suggests the recent election outcomes may not bode well for Newsom, as his chances of winning the Democratic presidential nomination plunged to just 7% in prediction markets. 

Newsom said this month’s election results have placed an obligation on his party to deliver.

“I’m particularly pleased with the outcome of the election, and I think the vast majority of people around the globe are very pleased with the outcome of the election as well,” he said.

For the second consecutive year, the Trump administration did not send a delegation to the annual summit, according to Newsom’s office.

Newsom’s travels also drew a jab from Democratic political strategist Steve Maviglio, who contrasted Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra’s efforts to ingratiate himself with Democratic lawmakers in Sacramento to the outgoing governor’s focus.

“This will be a refreshing change. A Governor who spends time working with the legislature instead of junkets to Turkey,” Maviglio wrote on X.

Newsom has played coy about his presidential ambitions, openly discussing the possibility while leaving himself room to walk away.

In September, Newsom told CNN’s Jake Tapper that he would sit out the 2028 race if former Vice President Kamala Harris entered.

“I don’t know if she runs, but we’ll see,” Newsom said during a fly-fishing interview in Montana. “I wouldn’t run if she ran.”

The claim elicited more than a few eyerolls among those in both Democratic and Republican political circles. But Newsom described a showdown between him and Harris as “mutual assured destruction,” pointing to their overlapping networks of friends and supporters.

Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters 

Newsom also said his wife and children would have to support a campaign.

“If they’re not on board,” he said, “that’s a non-starter.”
news.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom revealed his timetable to decide in a 2028 presidential run during a trip to an international climate conference in Turkey.
news.author: Josh Koehn

news.title: Democrat Cindy Holscher Wins Kansas Governor’s Race
news.text:
Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher has won the Kansas governor’s race, beating Kansas state Senate President Ty Masterson, a Republican.

Holscher, who ran on a campaign of increasing public school funding, lowering property taxes, and expanding Medicaid, won 50.3 percent of the vote compared to Masterson’s 49.7 percent. The Associated Press called the race on Nov. 12.

Up until the final days of the election, Masterson and Holscher were within 2 percentage points of one another in polling. Masterson held a slight lead, with some predictions showing him with around a 65 percent chance of winning.

Current Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly, a Democrat, was unable to seek another term because of term limits. However, in federal elections, Kansas has been largely Republican for decades.

Despite party differences, both candidates proposed deductions in homeowners’ property taxes and highlighted affordability concerns for Kansas voters.

Both focused on improving Kansas education, and both campaigned on attracting businesses and creating more jobs for Kansas.

According to recent polling, disapproval of President Donald Trump has alienated some in Kansas. Top among their concerns are higher prices and the war in Iran.

Trump carried the state in all three of his presidential campaigns, and took it with 57 percent of the vote in 2024.

Some Kansas Republicans seem to have rejected Trump’s sway over the party, and several told The Epoch Times that they switched their votes to Democrats in this election to avoid supporting the president.

Dennis, a voter from Overland Park who declined to share his last name, told The Epoch Times that he is a Republican, but voted for Democrats in both the Senate and governor’s races.

“I’ve been voting Democratic ever since Trump was elected,” Dennis said. “I’m a Bob Dole, Dwight Eisenhower Republican, not a Trumper.”

When asked if he was aware of the shift by his state to the left, Dennis said he believes it’s attributable to dislike of Trump’s policies.

Kelly’s wins in 2018 and 2024 seem to show a path for Democrats to take the state in a Democratic direction. However, in 2020 and 2024, former President Joe Biden and Kamala Harris each only carried the same five counties, among them, the largest in the state: Johnson and Shawnee.

Johnson County voter Deborah Brand is a registered Republican and former Republican committee chairperson, but she has voted largely for Democrats since Trump’s election.

She said she voted for Democrats in the gubernatorial and Senate elections this year because she felt the state “needs checks and balances” that it doesn’t currently have.

However, she said she doesn’t believe that the state’s swing to the left is necessarily permanent.

“Kansas has always been very Republican. I think if there were a decent candidate, they would remain Republican,” she said.
news.summary: Holscher replaces Gov. Laura Kelly, a Democrat who was unable to run again due to term limits.
news.author: Savannah Hulsey Pointer

news.title: Beto O’Rourke Says He’d “Do Anything” for James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa—Including Work for Them
news.text:
“Should I have talked to Joe Hagan when he was on my front porch in 2019?” O’Rourke says now, looking back at the cover story I wrote, in which he proclaimed he was “just born to be in it,” a premature declaration that almost immediately sank his prospects. “I’m glad I did. I’m grateful for everything that’s happened, because look where we are. It’s a beautiful new day in America.”
Like Stacey Abrams in Georgia, who lost her own race for governor but used her visibility to build a stronger coalition, O’Rourke can claim some credit for setting the table for Democratic success in Texas. Talarico won his first race, for a Republican-held state House seat, on O’Rourke’s 2018 wave. And as it turns out, O’Rourke himself weighed another Senate run this year. When Talarico asked whether he’d run, O’Rourke said only if Talarico ran for governor instead, eventually stepping aside after concluding that the moment called for “something and someone new.” When he launched his Senate campaign, Talarico said he wanted to replicate O’Rourke’s “energy.”
O’Rourke, meanwhile, became a behind-the-scenes player: Powered by People was one of four partners in the Texas Democrats’ $30 million coordinated campaign, and it says it reached more than 110,000 new and young voters in Texas this cycle. Ken Paxton noticed and tried to put O’Rourke “behind bars” for funding the Democrats who fled the state to block its Donald Trump–backed redistricting.
O’Rourke says the wave cascaded so far down the ballot in Texas that a candidate who tried backing out of her campaign before Election Day ended up winning. “At that point it was too late to take her name off the ballot,” he says. “She didn’t campaign, just won her election. That speaks to the magnitude of the wave, but also to the value of having a fighter on every front. Somebody said to me, ‘A wave’s great, even better if you have a surfboard.’”
Over an hour-long conversation, O’Rourke parses the political revolution in his home state, suggests how Democrats can hold on to their land grab, and, perhaps unsurprisingly, looks ahead to another run for office.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Vanity Fair: The conventional wisdom is that this was a revolt against Trump, and that the candidates and the Democratic strategy were secondary. What’s your read?
Beto O’Rourke: So much of this election was a rejection of Trump and Trumpism: the corruption, the wars, the cruelty. But after 2024, people were anxious that we didn’t have a unifying national leader. [Joe] Biden was not going to be it. Kamala Harris turned out not to be it. President Obama, I think wisely, held back…. Chuck Schumer was persona non grata in any gathering of Democrats. The DNC was in the red.
What it did was allow for candidates in different parts of the country to really establish themselves in their own right and by their own merits, never having to fear being under the shadow of a larger figure. It’s really a blessing. That’s how you get Abdul El-Sayed, James Talarico, Mary Peltola, all these extraordinary candidates who are extraordinarily different from each other. In Texas, for the first time in half a century, Democrats fielded a fighter on every front: 150 state House candidates, 38 congressional candidates, 16 state Senate candidates. You had to have a historically terrible, corrupt president. But you also had to have this historically beaten-down Democratic Party; that the Democrats don’t have a message, they don’t have a leader. That all turned out to be a great thing.
A year ago you convened Talarico, Colin Allred, and Joaquin Castro to think about a statewide slate. Talarico went his own way. You warned him he’d “want friends on that ticket.” What did you mean?
I just wanted to win, and I put that before anything else. James and I had many conversations before he officially announced. He asked me, “Are you interested? Would you run?” And I told him, “The only condition on which I would run is if you were to run for governor, or somebody else who could draw that kind of attention and resources, and if we had the ticket rounded out by strong contenders for every position on the ballot.”
My advice to him was: “Look, I’ve done this before. No matter how talented you are, no matter how much you can raise, this state is so big, the Republicans are so entrenched, you need a fighter on every front.” And ultimately, that’s what happened. Gina really hit her stride at the right time. Her strength as a candidate a year ago compared to how she finished is worlds apart, and that is a testament to what an exceptional leader she is.
Clearly, it was the right call for James to be there. He is just an extraordinarily talented communicator. He was a phenomenally focused candidate. He was absolutely the right guy for the moment. I also think it was the right call for Jasmine Crockett to run too. I know from being on college campuses how electrifying she is, how many young people she brought into the electorate this time. They stayed in even after Jasmine was defeated in the primary.
The Atlantic reported that you told Hinojosa, “Not one person can win Texas. It has to be two.” Is that what you said?
I definitely spoke to Gina before she made the decision to run, and then after. To be honest with you, I can’t remember if I said “two.” What I said consistently to everybody who was thinking about it—Colin, Joaquin, Gina, Jasmine [Crockett], James—was that you need a fighter on every front and the strongest possible ticket. That was based on the last run I had, in 2022, and even the ’18 run. If Joaquin or Julián Castro had run for governor when I was running for Senate, who knows? Of course, at that time, we didn’t know the size of the wave that was about to crash.
So you stepped aside.
I definitely did. I could have run…. You’d have to ask James, but I think he probably would have supported that if I had. We have an amazing organization in waiting, volunteers who’ve been with me, the ability to raise money. But was that the right thing to do? No. I had been before Texas twice before, and the moment demanded something different and, I would argue, something better.
You can’t discount a politician’s ambition and ego. I had to find a way to get past that. It helped having conversations with my wife. It helped having conversations with our kids. It helped having conversations with people who’d been on these runs with me before. Also, I spent a lot of time traveling Texas. My love language is a town hall meeting, where it’s just a free-for-all and anybody can step to the mic and ask any questions. At the end of that, I really felt this moment called for something and someone new. I don’t know that Texas could have produced a stronger—I was going to say candidate, but really a one-two punch. It was James and Gina. They’re both exceptional individually. Together, they transcended what had happened in politics for as long as I’ve been alive.
Honestly, my own doubt about whether Texas could be won was based on you. We’d seen this story before.
I wouldn’t have done this work as a volunteer for the last four years if I didn’t believe in Texas. I know in my heart and in my bones that we are so much better than the people in power. It’s the obscene abortion ban that has cost the lives of girls and women, the $7.25-an-hour minimum wage, the fact that we’re the least insured state in the country. Four years after Uvalde, and no one in power has done a single thing. It’s insane having Texas Republicans say, if you’re Muslim, regardless of whether you’re an immigrant, you should be deported from this country. That’s just not who we are.
When I ran for governor, 9 million registered voters didn’t cast a ballot. It’s not because they don’t care; it’s not that they’re lazy. This state makes it harder than any other to participate, so we’ve got to try that much harder. I knew it was a matter of time and effort. The greater the effort, the shorter the time. But did I know it would be 2026? Did I know it would be every statewide office and the state House? Fuck no, man. Nobody knew that.
Ken Paxton called you a “repeat loser” and tried to prosecute your PAC. He lost by 12 points.
We’ve spent more than $600,000; we have Powered by People defending our organization, defending me. He accused me of bribery. He tried to remove the license for Powered by People to do voter-registration work in the state of Texas. He promised to lock me up, to put me behind bars. The 15th Court of Appeals [judges], all of whom were appointed by Greg Abbott, so none of them friends of mine, have ruled against Paxton for attacking somebody for exercising their First Amendment rights. Do I think that I’m going to get that money back? I don’t know.
But how did you feel seeing him lose?
Couldn’t have happened to a better person.
Did Talarico and Hinojosa acknowledge your role, or did they keep their distance?
You’d have to ask them. I got a really nice message from James on election night, and I had a chance to campaign with Gina in the closing days of the election. That’s not an easy choice for Gina, right? Both of them did an exceptional job of being themselves and not seeming to be beholden to anybody. They invited nobody in from outside of Texas, and we all understood: This is their show. So getting to campaign with Gina here at the University of Texas at El Paso, at the University of Houston, it was really nice to hear her acknowledge the work that so many of us have been doing, especially all these volunteers who’ve been out there, whose names most people will never know.
I’ve known them both for a decade. James and I were on the campaign trail together in 2017 and 2018, when he was running his first race for state House in Williamson County. Somebody just sent me a picture of the two of us at an event in Williamson in 2017. These are really fucking good human beings, and they’re also really good at understanding power and how to win it. It is so rare that those two things come together.
Are Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries the right leaders for this moment?
Chuck Schumer absolutely is not. Early 2025, [Elon] Musk is running wild with DOGE, Trump is steamrolling every center of power. They’re all bending the knee—the Ivy Leagues, the big law firms, the media companies. Hakeem marshaled every Democratic vote in the House but one to stop Trump, DOGE, and Musk, and the deal with Schumer was going to do the same. Then, inexplicably, Schumer bent the knee as well. In that moment, it was absolutely over for me.
Schumer deserves so much credit and praise for his work over the decades. But he doesn’t deserve to be majority leader at this major turning point for the country, not when you have James Talarico, Abdul El-Sayed, or Jon Ossoff. We have an embarrassment of talent in the Senate right now, and we should use it. The age when any American cares what the majority leader reads on the Senate floor is over. I don’t even know what his message is, and that says something.
Hakeem Jeffries hasn’t had the chance to lead as Speaker. We were elected in the same class in 2012, and I’m grateful that he stood strong early in the Trump administration. I wish he could communicate more effectively than he has so far. Maybe there’s a scenario where he’s Speaker, but he taps the far better communicators in his caucus, like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, to do more of that work, and he’s focused on getting the legislative results.
Eleven House Democrats missed the vote to impeach [Pete] Hegseth, enough to have changed the outcome. What happened there?
Eleven is a big number. That certainly invites some conspiracy thinking, or, maybe just as bad, the idea that these folks aren’t up to the job. It’s really important that the Democratic leadership in the House address this directly, explain what happened, and take ownership and responsibility for it.
You’ve said Democrats wasted their power in 2009 and 2021, and that next time they should “drive that car like we stole it.” What happens in the first 100 days?
Right off the bat, you have to make our lives better in a way that we can feel. In Texas, that’s not hard, because we are in such a fucking hole. Raise the minimum wage from $7.25. Expand Medicaid when the federal government’s paying 90 cents on the dollar. Stop this voucher thing that is draining tax dollars from local schools, and pay teachers so they don’t have to work a second or third job.
Nationally, you have to do the same. The response to this from many is that Trump has the power of the pen and will veto that. Make him veto that. I don’t like anything about him, but I don’t know that there’s a more successful political operator than Trump. I don’t think there’s someone who reads power better than he does. Maybe there are deals to be had. Maybe you force the veto, and you set up a clear contrast going into 2028. At a minimum, you have to get caught trying.
The huge issues that Democrats have absolutely failed to lead on, we have to lead on now, so that would include immigration and that would include democracy. Immigration was arguably the issue that voters made their decisions on in 2016 and 2024, and if we continue to hope that it’s just going to solve itself, instead of making tough choices and using political capital on this, then it’s going to be our demise in future elections as well. [On democracy], there’s no democracy to restore or save. There is a democracy you can build anew. Getting corporations out of politics; what just passed in Montana is potentially a wonderful precedent from which we could build. Getting a voting rights act passed again. [Pushing] the popular-vote compact; I think we have enough trifectas now. I’m probably in the minority in the Democratic Party, but I’m a big believer in term limits. People give a speech and are like, “We’ve got to overturn Citizens United,” or, “We’ve got to do away with the Electoral College.” That’s a great applause line, but when is that ever going to happen?
The big dig on Democrats is: You talked a great game on immigration, then you won the White House; you had the House and the Senate. You didn’t do anything. You talked a great game about voting rights. You had the trifecta, and you didn’t do anything. Now we have the power. We’d better deliver, or watch out.
I’m surprised I’m not hearing more from you about prosecutions and subpoenas. You spent the last two years warning about fascism and calling for accountability.
That’s got to be part of it too. The law is king in this country; no one’s above it, no one’s below it. We’ve allowed the precedent, through the Epstein crimes, that you can be rich enough and well-connected enough to rape and traffic girls and women with complete impunity. I spent a lot of time with young people doing this voter-registration work, and that is probably the number one thing I hear from them for why they don’t vote: This shit doesn’t work. Ghislaine Maxwell [went to jail], but no man who actually did this has gone to prison or even faced trial.
Then there’s the corruption that flows from the president through his family, through his Cabinet officials, through the oligarchs [with whom] he surrounds himself. If we let this stand, much the way that we let stand his crimes against this country on January 6, 2021, that sets the most dangerous precedent. Look at the Roman Republic. It wasn’t Caesar crossing the Rubicon. It was Sulla turning his armies against Rome, and there was never a consequence or accountability for that, so the precedent was set and Caesar picked that up. [Editor’s note: O’Rourke is an avid fan of the podcast The Rest Is History.] There will be a more capable, powerful demagogue than Trump—he or she may be a Democrat; he or she may be a Republican—who will use that precedent unless that door is closed. I know this is an unpopular thing to talk about within our party, because folks want to turn the page. But that keeps biting us in the ass. Everyone who went to prison for [January 6] was pardoned by this president.
But if you spend the next two years investigating him and prices stay high, Democrats are cooked.
That’s exactly right. That’s why I said you’ve got to deliver for people, and they have to feel it immediately. Democrats are responsible for so many good things that are both slow-working and expressed through the tax code, like the child tax credit, and for which they don’t claim credit. Those things have to change.
I was in the Rio Grande Valley after 2020, doing voter registration, knocking on doors, and talking to this guy who voted for Trump. I said, “You had a front-row seat to kids in cages, to family separation, to this cruelty here. Tell me what’s going on.” And he said, “I hate all that stuff, but voting on those issues when I can’t feed my family and I may lose my home is a luxury. I don’t have that luxury.” We have to learn that lesson. You’ve got to make people’s lives better, and if you do that, you build trust and legitimacy: “Okay, these guys are really helping me. They really reflect my values and my interests. And now that they are pursuing these investigations and this accountability, I trust them, and I know that, regardless of the outcome of these investigations, my life is better because they are in power.”
If Trump felt that he or his family were under real legal threat, is there any world in which investigations become a chip to trade, say, for immigration reform? I realize this is very Trumpy thinking, but you are dealing with Trump.
No. Totally understandable, and it’s a recognition of how politics and power typically work. But part of how we got Trump in the first place was that there weren’t consequences for massive failures or crimes committed: these banks that were bailed out after they had driven so many Americans into poverty and homelessness in 2008 and 2009, these wars the Bush administration launched on false pretenses. They lied to us, they lied to the world, and it took the lives of so many Americans, Iraqis, and Afghans. Never any consequence or accountability.
This corruption has been so flagrant, it’s as though Trump and those closest to him were daring America to hold them accountable. Then there’s the open defiance of the law and the Constitution: killing people on fishing boats in the Caribbean, kidnapping a head of state, launching a war and continuing it in violation of the War Powers Act. When you allow these things to stand, they become the precedent. But if there’s accountability, then that becomes the precedent upon which future leaders will be able to act. Trump may feel he’s fighting for his life, that he’s backed into a corner. He may make it harder for Democrats to do the things that they need to do. But I don’t think we can operate in fear of him.
Some Democrats, like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, argue that the corruption and the high prices are the same story. Do you buy that?
Talarico is masterful at saying that: Their corruption is costing you and your family. So many examples in Texas. Billionaires bought off Governor Greg Abbott and persuaded him to pursue a voucher scheme that took public dollars out of local schools and sent them to private schools, decreased the quality of your school, and raised your local property taxes to make up the difference. Abbott, beholden to corporate interests, opened the door [to data centers], and our electricity prices went up and the quality of our water and air was compromised.
The biggest one was in 2021, when we had the winter storm. In the energy capital of the world, they couldn’t keep the lights on or the power running, and pipeline operators [and others in the energy industry], among the biggest donors to Greg Abbott, began to price-gouge, bankrupting utilities and causing ratepayers to pay sky-high prices. One of the pipeline operator CEOs wrote Abbott a $1 million check at the end of that winter storm, almost as if to say thank you for not prosecuting them. It’s not corruption in an abstract way; it’s corruption that’s costing you. And yes, that corruption should be prosecuted. It’s not enough to just win the election and throw the bums out. If the bums broke the law, then they have to face the consequences.
If Democrats hold this ground, it would seem to open the door for you again. Is there an office you can imagine running for in 2028 or 2030?
I don’t know, and people would have to answer that question for me. That’s what I’ve been trying to do these last four years, just listen to people and figure out where I can be most useful. I’ve tried to remain agnostic.
I had a conversation earlier in the year with somebody who just won in Texas, and they had been one of the people to encourage me to run for governor in 2022—what the fuck was I thinking, running in Joe Biden’s midterm?—and I asked them, “Did you think I had any chance to win?” And they said, “Oh God, no.” But they knew that we needed somebody to galvanize the state, protect our gains in Harris County, and shore up the wins that we’d [earned] in 2018. Somebody had to carry us through that next stage of the relay.
Just so I’m clear, I would not have run if I didn’t think there was a chance we could win in 2022. It was an incredibly tough environment that got tougher and tougher as the race proceeded. But it did a lot of good, and in some small way it was probably helpful toward what happened in 2026.
When [my wife] Amy and I made the decision in 2016 that we had to do something, I went to everyone: Joaquin and Julián Castro, Clay Jenkins, Michael Sorrell, Wendy Davis. I asked each of them, “Will you run? If you do, I will get behind you.” Ultimately, I was like, “Okay, if you guys aren’t going to do it, I am going to do it. I know this is crazy, and I know all of you are better positioned, I’m going to do it.” So if I feel the way that I felt that time, that I’m the right person for this, then, whatever the odds, I’m going to get out there. But if running could hurt us, if there’s somebody better—and that was a conclusion I drew coming into this cycle—then please step up, and I’ll get out of the way and support you as a volunteer.
The next statewide race in Texas is 2030. One thing I’m thinking about right now is 2028, and the fact that the 40 Electoral College votes in Texas are ours to lose. I want to be part of the team getting Texas ready for that nominee to win our state. I’m happy to follow James and Gina’s lead. They’re our leaders now.
Can you imagine working in a Hinojosa administration?
I will do anything for her, and the same for James. It’s just crazy, hearing that.
What about taking Powered by People to Florida? They could use some help, evidently.
These states of the former Confederacy have worked so hard to make it hard for people, especially young people, to vote. We don’t have Election Day data yet, but through early voting, 60% of our voters, overwhelmingly 18 to 29 years old, voted through early voting. That’s about 33 points ahead of the average for that demographic in Texas. I sure wish our party had put resources behind [Angie] Nixon and [David] Jolly in Florida. We could have won those races. What was [the margin] in the governor’s race? 1.3%. Heartbreaking. If I can be useful there, I’m happy to go.
About a year after my 2019 story came out, I texted you that I hoped there were no hard feelings, and you took responsibility for your own errors. It seems like you’ve been through a process since then.
That’s just life, right? I truly feel so incredibly lucky: getting to serve in Congress, getting to run for the US Senate, being considered for the nomination in 2020, being back out on the trail for governor, and then doing this work with Powered by People. When I get depressed is when I don’t have purpose. Then I’m prone to feel sorry for myself or to wonder what if. I’m a big believer that action is the antidote to despair. So I try not to dwell too much on decisions that I’ve made. Should I have talked to Joe Hagan when he was on my front porch in 2019? I’m glad I did. I’m grateful for everything that’s happened, because look at where we are. It’s a beautiful new day in America.
Joe Rogan suggested on his podcast that Talarico should run for president. Any advice for him?
I am the last guy to give Talarico advice, because he’s just been so freaking smart and amazing. Whether he runs for president, whether he serves out his full term in the Senate, he is one of very few leaders in this country who have met the moment. I trust him to make the best decisions for, first and foremost, the country, for Texas, and then for himself.
Who excites you in the 2028 field? You’ve got Gavin Newsom on the center-left, and AOC and Ro Khanna presenting themselves as heirs to Bernie Sanders.
We could have added another 15 people to that list. There was a lot of gnashing of teeth two years ago: We don’t have a national leader; what is Democrats’ message? That was liberating for all of these candidates, and you’re going to have so many diverse perspectives in 2028. What you did these last 10 years is going to be an important consideration. Gavin Newsom was one of the first national Democrats to recognize what Trump was trying to do by redrawing these congressional maps, starting in Texas, and I was really impressed with how quickly he moved and how strong he was on offense. Pete Buttigieg has been nonstop traveling the country supporting candidates. In the wake of 2024, with this sense of total defeat, a few people just got out there, and AOC was one of them. I like the folks who never stop fighting, who are true to themselves and not susceptible to the prevailing winds. Bernie Sanders is probably the best example of that.
Ro Khanna and I, when we were in Congress together, authored the No PAC Act. We asked our legislative staffs, “Can you find out who last authored a bill like this so we can amend it and improve it and make it our own?” There was no bill. Nobody had ever done that. He’s been so consistently focused on democracy. Greg Casar, he’s from Texas. He’s the chair of the [Congressional] Progressive Caucus and also has been crisscrossing the country. There are a lot of good people out there.
After 2016 and 2024, a lot of women I know concluded that this country won’t elect a woman president. Can a woman be elected?
Absolutely. Gina Hinojosa—here in Texas, the conventional wisdom was that if a Democrat ever wins, it’s got to be a straight white man who fits the following characteristics. And here you have the first Latina from the border. It’s fucking awesome. It’s going to sound corny, but I really believe in this country, and that faith was vindicated last Tuesday. It wasn’t the country being like, “Go Democrats!” It was the country saying, “We can do better, and we’re going to take a chance on folks who may not fit the profile.” I think that holds true for the country in 2028.
You just turned 54. If you never ran again, would you be okay with that?
I think about it sometimes. Is the prize the office—junior senator from the state of Texas, president of the United States of America? Or is the prize a much better world for my kids and this country? I always want that to be the answer, and it is. I just fucking won the lottery in life. Our kids are absolutely thriving; my oldest is about to be 20, middle kid is 18, my youngest just turned 16. I’ve been lucky with Amy and living in El Paso, getting to do this fulfilling work.
But just to be clear: Would I love to serve in office again at some point? Absolutely. The El Paso City Council may have been my most fulfilling time in politics. Loved being in Congress—what a high honor. But if it doesn’t happen, I’m more than okay. I’m the luckiest guy out there. I’m good, no matter what happens.
news.summary: The Texas politician, whose own presidential and Senate bids have failed, has thrown himself into organizing. In conversation with Joe Hagan, he examines the 2026 midterms—and his future prospects.

news.title: Alsobrooks proves her mettle by pressing yet another Trump nominee
news.text:
Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., has developed quite a reputation for flaying Donald Trump’s nominees during their confirmation hearings.

Catherine Eschbach, Trump’s pick for general counsel of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, just made the list, which also includes Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Assistant Health Secretary Brian Christine.

Trump wants Eschbach, currently the EEOC’s acting general counsel, to be the agency’s top lawyer. The EEOC is designed to uphold civil rights in the workplace, but Trump allies have perverted it into a vehicle for their bigoted and baseless conspiracy theories about systemic workplace discrimination harming white men.

At her Senate confirmation hearing Tuesday, Eschbach repeatedly deflected Alsobrooks’ questions about one of her direct reports: an EEOC lawyer who essentially became a men’s rights activist after receiving a 2½-year suspension from Catholic University following a fellow student’s allegation of sexual assault.

The lawyer, Benjamin North, has denied the allegation and said the encounter was consensual. In 2017, he filed a lawsuit against Catholic University that ended with a stipulated dismissal.

Alsobrooks, a former prosecutor who specialized in domestic violence cases, asked Eschbach whether she knew about North’s school suspension and whether it’s appropriate for someone credibly accused of sexual assault to lead cases at the EEOC.

The nominee didn’t seem to want to address either question head-on. Instead, she repeatedly asserted that, in obtaining his law license, North had proved to the Virginia State Bar that he was of “good moral character.”

news.title: Arnold reveals why he refused to campaign for Trump in 2016
news.text: Actor and former California Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger has revealed why he refused to campaign for Donald Trump during his 2016 presidential run, despite sharing a close friendship with him at the time. Appearing on Jimmy Kimmel Live! on Wednesday, November 11, Schwarzenegger said Trump's views on climate change and pollution went against everything he had worked towards for years. The 79-year-old actor also spoke about why he continues to identify as a traditional Republican despite disagreeing with the party's present-day direction, urging Democrats and Republicans to work together rather than prioritising party politics.Schwarzenegger, who became California's governor in November 2003, recalled that Trump had personally approached him during his 2016 presidential campaign, asking him to endorse his candidacy and campaign alongside him. The two had shared a good relationship, but Schwarzenegger said he could not support Trump because of their differences over environmental issues."We had a good relationship; we were very good friends. He asked me if I would go and endorse him and campaign with him," Schwarzenegger told Jimmy Kimmel.Recalling his response, he said he told Trump that although he wanted to remain friends, he disagreed with several things the businessman-turned-politician stood for.Schwarzenegger specifically pointed to Trump's position on climate change and pollution, explaining that environmental protection had been an important part of his own work for years."I said, 'You don't believe there is climate change. You don't believe the threat of pollution,'" he recalled, adding that pollution kills millions of people and cannot simply be ignored.He further said that he could not campaign for Trump because of that issue alone.Why Schwarzenegger still considers himself a traditional RepublicanDuring the conversation, Kimmel also asked Schwarzenegger whether he still considered himself a Republican despite his disagreements with the party's current political direction."Yeah, I'm a Republican, absolutely," he replied.Explaining what being a traditional Republican means to him, Schwarzenegger referred to the party's historical role in ending slavery and granting African Americans citizenship and voting rights.When Kimmel pointed out that these values appeared to be at odds with what the modern Republican Party represents, Schwarzenegger responded that he did not need to change his own philosophy.He also cited former US presidents Ronald Reagan and Richard Nixon, crediting Reagan with establishing California's Air Resources Board and Nixon with creating the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)."Those are the kind of Republicans that used to go and work together with the Democrats and got things done. This is the kind of Republican that I am," he explained.Schwarzenegger urges Democrats and Republicans to work togetherThe actor also spoke about the growing political divide in the United States and said neither party had done enough to address major issues despite repeatedly gaining power.Referring to the Democrats' recent midterm gains, Schwarzenegger described the political shift as a "tidal wave or a tsunami" rather than simply a blue wave. He argued that political power keeps moving between Democrats and Republicans, but important problems remain unresolved.He specifically mentioned immigration reform, national debt and healthcare, saying successive administrations and lawmakers had failed to find lasting solutions.Schwarzenegger also expressed support for immigration reform and a healthcare system that ensures everyone has coverage. During the conversation, he disagreed with Kimmel over the Affordable Care Act, describing it as a well-intentioned attempt that had not adequately addressed rising healthcare costs.He maintained that neither party could achieve meaningful progress by acting alone."What you have to do is the Democrats and the Republicans have to work together like we did when I was governor of California," he said.He further emphasised that elected representatives should focus on serving citizens rather than their political parties."You have to get together and accomplish and be a public servant rather than a party servant. There's a difference," he added.Schwarzenegger had endorsed Kamala Harris in 2024Despite identifying as a Republican, Schwarzenegger has previously taken positions that put him at odds with the party's presidential leadership. During the 2024 US presidential election, he publicly endorsed Democratic candidate Kamala Harris and her running mate Tim Walz.His latest remarks reinforce his position that political beliefs should not necessarily be dictated by party loyalty. The actor has repeatedly spoken about the importance of environmental protection and bipartisan cooperation.Schwarzenegger appeared on Jimmy Kimmel Live! to promote his upcoming film The Man With the Bag. His conversation with Kimmel covered his Hollywood career, political identity, friendship with Trump and his views on the changing Republican Party.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
news.summary: Arnold Schwarzenegger has revealed that he refused to campaign for Donald Trump during his 2016 presidential run despite their friendship, citing disagreements over climate change and pollution. Appearing on Jimmy Kimmel Live!, the former California governor reaffirmed his Republican identity and urged Democrats and Republicans to work together, prioritising public service over party politics.

news.title: Here is the voting bloc that ‘despises’ Trump
news.text:
President Donald Trump may “hate” his enemies, but new midterm data suggests one group of voters increasingly “despises” him.

CNN data analyst Harry Enten discussed the sharp decline in Trump's support among voters aged 18 to 24 during a Thursday conversation with anchor Kate Bolduan. He pointed to data showing the president's net approval rating among young voters had fallen from 43 percent in 2024 to just 15 percent this year.

“Look at this margin. Look at this margin. That is wild. Yeah, it’s huge. It’s a huge shift. I mean, that is like this isn’t over 20 years. This is over two years,” Enten said.

The shift marks a 28-point drop in Trump's standing with younger voters in just two years, Enten said.

“We are talking about a 28-point decline in terms of where he went from vote share to approval rating in just two years’ time,” he said. “This drove a historic shift away from the Republicans to the Democrats.”

“They, simply put, despised the president of the United States,” Enten added.

The decline follows a period when Trump made gains with younger voters. In 2020, Democratic presidential candidate Joe Biden held a 25-point advantage among young voters. Four years later, that advantage had narrowed to just four points when Kamala Harris faced Trump, according to research from Tufts University's Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement.

Trump also made gains among young men in 2024, winning their support by 14 points. His campaign actively courted this group, including through appearances on popular podcasts hosted by Joe Rogan and Theo Von. During those interviews, Trump discussed his policies, as well as topics such as cancel culture and the UFC.

But Enten said many young voters who gave Trump and Republicans a chance after 2024 became disillusioned with the administration over healthcare, rising costs and the Iran war. Their frustration helped drive record turnout among younger voters and a historic midterm victory for Democrats. 

“It is one of the big reasons why Democrats did so well during the election was younger voters who were giving ... a lot of them were giving Republicans a chance, but that chance Republicans squandered, and they said we’re going back in the other direction and we’re supporting Democrats in overwhelming numbers,” Enten said.

In an interview with CBS News’ “60 Minutes” following the midterms, Trump acknowledged that his administration’s immigration crackdown may have seemed “too tough” and may have alienated voters.

news.title: The GOP’s War Plan for Shattering the Democratic Party Coalition in 5 Easy Steps
news.text:
Yesterday we introduced a new political theory. Today we unleash it.

Quick refresher: Instead of trying to persuade voters, we’re now going to agree with them. (Even if we’ve gotta get creative.) Because the monoculture is dead, our country is hyper-fragmented, and there simply aren’t enough public squares or “arenas of ideas” to win hearts and minds. We’ve traded our public squares for echo chambers — and each echo chamber has its own media, social norms, consensus opinions, and guiding principles. (All enforced, of course, by algorithms.)

The GOP just spent billions trying to persuade audiences about the health of the economy. Meanwhile, the Democrats raced like Usain Bolt toward voters’ preexisting confirmation biases about inflation, affordability, gas prices, the “Epstein class,” Israel/AIPAC, and corruption. 

Advantage: Democrats.

After all, the likelihood of an outsider invading a foreign echo chamber and convincing the occupants to change their minds is infinitesimally small. Sure, if you spend enough money, you can (usually) buy your way in, but you’ll be outnumbered, drowned out, ridiculed, and marginalized. 

Home-field advantage is a killer.

You can elevate awareness, but you can’t gain acceptance. Nor will you win hearts and minds. (And if you push too hard, it’ll lead to ugly blowback, making everything worse.)

But if you stop arguing and tell them something they already believe, they’ll roll over and show you their belly.

Which led to our theory — and our new guiding PR principle: “Today’s political wars are won on the wings of confirmation bias.”

We’re no longer persuading. As of today, we’re agreeing.

Furthermore, because confirmation bias produces blind spots, we’re gonna figure out our opponents' blind spots and exploit them, too. (Cue evil laughter.)

Okay, fine. It’s an intriguing theory, Mr. Pinsker, but how the heck do we apply it?

Glad you asked. Below are five major Democratic blocs, each representing a critical component of the donkey’s coalition. This isn’t an exhaustive list, but it’s a pretty good start.

Let’s whack ‘em around like a piñata, one at a time!

Because, when you put the Democratic Party under the microscope, you see how fragile its coalition really is. This isn’t a party bound by bedrock principles, but a ragtag collection of special interest groups. 

The fault lines are obvious. So let’s get crackin’.

Group 1: Black voters. Lately, they’ve been barometers of Democratic enthusiasm. In 2024, their numbers dropped and Republicans won; in 2026, it was the opposite. Of all the Democrats' voting blocs, blacks have been the most loyal — and, very often, the most taken for granted.

It’s something they’re sensitive about, which is a useful nugget of information.

How to attack: Bombard their echo chambers with stories about the DSA’s lily-white complexion, hostility to Christianity, and indifference to black suffering.

I’ve written about the DSA’s abysmal lack of diversity, but I’m not the only one who’s noticed:

CNN: Hakeem Jeffries criticizes the DSA over lack of diversity when crowd of its members chanted “you’re next” at Jeffries “It was very interesting to me, as observed by others, that there was almost zero diversity in that crowd.” https://t.co/QuRHYq4cIJ— Politics & Poll Tracker 📡 (@PollTracker2024) November 8, 2026

The DSA is about to go to war with Hakeem Jeffries — because it’s a revolutionary movement, and that’s what revolutionary movements do. Yet Jeffries is about to make history as America’s first black speaker of the House.

Getcha popcorn ready!

It’s a juicy storyline: The DSA can’t yank the Dems to the radical left without playing hardball with Jeffries. The DSA movement needs drama, chaos, and conflict — for political purposes, organizational growth, and TikTok engagement. Its goal, after all, isn’t for Jeffries to succeed, but to sow the seeds of a socialist takeover.

So every single time the DSA screws over Jeffries, the GOP should tell black voters all about it: They’re taking you for granted again!

The pro-Islamic sensibilities of the DSA are also a friction point with black voters, who are disproportionately Christian: 73% of blacks are Christian, compared to 62% of whites. Blacks are also more likely than whites to attend church and engage in “religious practices.” Additionally, just 39% of whites called the Bible “very important,” compared to 70% of blacks, who are also about twice as likely to read the Bible and pray every day.

Which might be why blacks are also disproportionately pro-Israel.

From Fox News:

[A]ccording to the Fox News poll, African Americans were the racial group most likely to say the U.S. isn't supportive enough of Israel when asked the question along with White and Hispanic voters. That number was 25% compared with 19% for Hispanic voters and 15% for White voters.African American voters were also the least likely of the three groups to agree that America was too supportive of Israel, with 40% disagreeing as compared to White voters at 44% and Hispanic voters at 56%.

As the DSA dons a keffiyeh, pulls the Dems towards Mecca, and amplifies its anti-Israel hysteria, Republicans should grab a megaphone and speak directly to the black community: The DSA doesn’t care about you, Christianity, Hakeem Jeffries, or black people succeeding.

Because the DSA is not your friend.

Group 2: Socialists/DSA voters. In their opinion, they just won a yuuuge mandate to remake America — and anything short of a Marxist overhaul would be a letdown. They see Zohran Mamdani in New York City, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, and AOC getting ready to run for president: Finally, the socialist stars have aligned!

Lo and behold, their plan just might work!

How to attack: Tell ‘em that the DNC is controlled by evil corporations, the Democratic Party is rigged, and this conspiracy, alas, cannot be fixed via the electoral process.

The DSA wants to use the Democratic Party as a skinsuit. It never was an ideological partnership; this was ALWAYS a marriage of convenience.

So let’s make it more inconvenient.

Because their blind spot is their hysterical phobia of corporations, capitalism, billionaires, and conspiracies. In their minds, anything “they” touch is de facto tainted — including partisan politics.

Every time Jeffries’ side (a.k.a. the “corporatists,” “Zionists,” and “sellouts”) wins, invade DSA echo chambers and agree with ‘em: Obviously, they were right all along.

Nothing will change. This conspiracy is too deep. (Curse those rich Jews!) So what’s the point in even trying?

Demotivate them from trusting Democrats and/or working within the two-party system. 

Group 3: Islamic/anti-Israel voters. There’s considerable overlap between Islamic/anti-Israel voters and ordinary DSA voters, but there are also a few critical distinctions. For starters, plenty of communists and socialists are atheists; their north star is acquiring the “means of production” for economic reasons, not fulfilling Islamic conquests and religious prophecies. 

But millions of Islamic/anti-Israel voters couldn’t care less about economics. That’s not why they’re waving pro-Hamas signs, marching in the street, screaming about Jews, or voting Democrat.

Normally, I’d feel guilty engaging in this sort of tactic, because antisemitism sucks. But this is an unusual situation: Sen. Schumer was so desperate to regain power that he invited, funded, and welcomed Islamic/anti-Israel candidates into his party!

He would’ve still won a majority if he'd had the moral courage to disavow antisemitism — but he didn’t. And now, the problem is his.

Chuck Schumer is an old Jew with sky-high negatives who has previously been supportive of Israel and AIPAC. (He was one of just a handful of Democrats who voted against President Barack Obama’s Iran deal.)

And maybe next time, the DNC will think twice before partnering with bigots.

Group 4: Unmarried women voters. Ah, cat ladies. (Grocery stores should sell cat food, ice cream, and box wine together. How to attack: This might sound a bit unusual, but I’d zero in on mental health issues.

Because it’s something they’re already hypersensitive about. For younger liberal women, 50% admit to having a mental health condition. For older women, 25% are already on antidepressants.

We’re not going to change Karen’s mind about Trump, ICE, or the latest left-wing cause du jour, but we can demotivate her by highlighting how her lifestyle is destroying her mental health. ‘Cause that’s something she’d actually believe!

This is a bloc that’s fluent in therapy-speak and psychobabble. Half their friends have a therapist, a pill bottle, and a laundry list of disorders, conditions, phobias, and anxieties. They’re disproportionately lonely, depressed, and mentally ill.

Why not fund studies and surveys that link mental problems to liberalism’s sacred cows?

They’re predisposed to believe this stuff anyway. I’ll betcha a Diet Coke that a million-zillion Riley Gaines speeches would do less to demotivate ‘em from trans activism than just one “scientific study” that documents the mental health woes of trans kids — or the link between trans and mass shootings.

And a dedicated PR campaign of scientific studies? One right after the other?

That could REALLY have an impact.

Because that’s their blind spot: They know women are struggling with mental problems, and they’ve placed therapy on a pedestal. No matter the problem, therapy is always the solution. It’s the magic cure to all of life’s challenges.

So let’s tell ‘em a story they’re already predisposed to believe.

Group 5: Latino voters. They’re 19.5% of the population, and there are over a million of ‘em in key electoral states like Texas, Pennsylvania, North Carolina, Colorado, Georgia, and more. In 2024, President Trump made historic inroads with Latinos, but in 2026, they swung back to the Dems with gusto. Some outlets blamed the ICE raids for triggering the reversal.

I don’t blame the ICE raids for the loss of Latinos. In fact, given a choice between Trump’s ICE raids and Joe Biden’s open border, I’ll betcha most Latinos would prefer the ICE raids. 

Maybe ICE went too far, but Latinos tend to be less driven by ideology than by household issues. They’re Catholics with traditional, family-centric values; on census forms, many claim to be white, because they identify as white culturally, aspirationally, and through deliberate, intentional assimilation.

news.title: New Hamtramck mayor: Trump's immigration crackdown hurting city
news.text:
The new mayor of Hamtramck is concerned about the crackdown on immigration by the administration of President Donald Trump, saying it's affecting the city's ability to attract residents and maintain tax revenue.

Hamtramck Mayor Muhith Mahmood, sworn in Sunday, Nov. 8, told the Detroit Free Press about his concerns, noting that his city has long attracted immigrants to its diverse, walkable communities with easy access to necessities for newcomers who may not have a car. Almost 47% of the city's residents are immigrants, the highest among cities in Michigan, according to 2024 census data. He worries about the city defaulting if it can't continue to attract immigrants.

"Because of the immigration (policies) right now, the Donald Trump policies, there are no immigrants coming," Mahmood told the Free Press on Nov. 11. "That's hurting our future. I think it's going to hurt worse ... (the) next few months."

Mahmood is an immigrant from Bangladesh, who's Michigan's first Bangladeshi American mayor in state history.

"Hamtramck was built by the immigrant families," Mahmood said. "When they come, everything is close by: school, mosque, shop, bank, everything in walking distance. So that makes it more comfortable for people to stay in this city and do their daily living activities."

The previous two mayors, Adam Alharbi and Amer Ghalib, were also immigrants, but they were supportive of Trump, who rallied in Hamtramck in 2024. Ghalib, who endorsed Trump in 2024, met last year with Stephen Miller, a key architect of Trump's immigration crackdown, asking for immigration relief, and was named an adviser to Trump last month in October.

In November 2024, Trump got 43% of the vote in Hamtramck, amid concern about the war in Gaza and the Democrats' views on social issues. That was up from the 13% Trump got in 2020. But in this month's election, November 2026, Republican candidates Mike Rogers and John James each got only 7% of the vote in Hamtramck amid concern over Republican attacks against immigrants and Muslims. Mahmood is a Democrat who endorsed Kamala Harris in 2024.

Before 2025, it was difficult to find houses for rent in Hamtramck because there was high demand to live in the city, he said. But that has now changed since Trump became president again, with "House for Rent" signs increasingly staying up for long periods.

"When you drive through in Hamtramck, any houses you find, this is for rent," Mahmood said. "That's not ever happened before. So it is impacting our city big time."

Hamtramck had "one of the highest demand for renting ... but recently, with the Donald Trump policy, nobody is coming to America in the last few months," he said.

More: Arab, Muslim voters mobilized for election: 'The energy is different'

The population of Hamtramck jumped 27% from 2010 to 2020 as immigrants and their children grew the city. But from 2020 to July 2025, the population has dropped 4.1%, according to census data. Mahmood is concerned that the population decline may continue, resulting in less tax revenue for the city, where 40% of the working-class residents live below the poverty line.

Hamtramck is a densely populated city, which makes it "convenient for people when they come from out of country," Mahmood said. "It takes time for them to (get their) driving license."

In Hamtramck, residents can walk to places like the Social Security office, banks and houses of worship.

"Everything is walking distance," he said.

If the immigration crackdown continues, "we're ... going to default ... we're going to get hit hard," Mahmood said at Tuesday's council meeting, his first since becoming mayor. Mahmood was previously a city councilman.

On Sunday, Mahmood was sworn in by Judge Alexis Krot at the Hamtramck Community Center at an inauguration attended by many of his supporters in the Bangladeshi immigrant community and others.

The White House did not return a message seeking comment about concerns that its immigration policies are hurting Hamtramck, where Trump and Republicans campaigned in 2024.

High water bills affecting residents

Another challenge facing the city's ability to retain residents is high water bills. Mahmood and some city council members have voiced concerns about the rising cost of water for residents.

Part of the problem is the aging infrastructure of the city's water lines that need repairs. The council debated Tuesday some resolutions on approving tax dollars to make repairs. Some were approved, and others were not.

Mahmoud said his father-in-law last month got a water bill of $250.

 "Our water bill is too high, extremely very high," Mahmoud said.

Mahmoud has asked the city to form a subcommittee to explore ways to lower water bills for residents.

news.title: Trump's staff are so fed up they're now admitting the truth about his close aide Natalie Harp and the White House's revolving door of young, inexperienced women: MAUREEN CALLAHAN
news.text:
Here we are, in the waning days of Donald Trump's presidency, MAGA thumped and perhaps destroyed forever by last week's midterms, and our commander in chief seems less concerned with his legacy than with the revolving door of young, attractive, politically inexperienced women who comport themselves as fan girls.

Groupies, really.

Is this how Trump wants to go down in the history books?

It's incredible — and incredibly self-destructive — when you think about it: The candidate who was nearly undone, days before the 2016 election, by the Access Hollywood 'grab 'em by the p***y' tape; who staged the greatest political comeback in history by running, in large part, as a protector of women in 2024 who would close the border to violent predators who murdered Jocelyn Nungaray and Laken Riley, and would get biological men out of female sports and spaces — well, it seems that version of Trump is long gone.

Now he's more like a modern-day King Henry VIII, only he just banishes the women he tires of rather than beheading them.

The latest to inflame the otherwise serious people in Trump's orbit: Natalie Harp, a 35-year-old former television personality who has most recently made headlines after a 'mystery woman' was caught giggling in the background as Trump spoke on the phone, live, to C-SPAN on Monday night. We don't know for sure that it was Harp, but we know she often helps field calls on Trump's personal cell.

So: Democrats sweep the House and the Senate, mobilize to impeach Trump's Secretary of War, investigate alleged corruption among his family members and appointees — and Trump seems increasingly preoccupied with Harp, who reportedly takes no days off and recently moved into the President's dining room to work.

Harp's detractors call her 'the human printer', because she carries an actual printer with her as she accompanies the President everywhere.

She has chased after him on golf courses, literally running behind his golf cart. She has written him devotional letters, passages of which were published by the New York Times.

'I never want to bring you anything but joy,' Harp wrote. 'You are all that matters to me.'

She also wrote to Trump that she considers him to be her 'Guardian and Protector in this life.'

It was Harp who sat with Trump in the White House private residence watching last week's midterm results. Melania was not there and reportedly did not watch.

Meanwhile, the only other woman with Trump that night was his Chief of Staff Susie Wiles — infamously loyal, the woman said to have gotten Trump elected in 2024, against all odds, and then continued working while battling cancer.

Wiles, who Trump reportedly threw out of the Oval Office on November 5, yelling at her and blaming her for the midterm rout. Wiles — who does not physically resemble many of Trump's other female advisers — submitted her resignation before he could fire her.

By contrast, Politico reported in September that Trump gave Harp $45,000 as a 'cash gift for the holidays' — this on top of her $150,000 taxpayer-funded salary as executive assistant to the President.

Harp appears to have replaced Laura Loomer, the conspiracy theorist who thinks 9/11 was an 'inside job' — but who was, in 2024, right by Trump's side at that year's September 11 memorial anyway. She also made at least one racist comment against Kamala Harris, saying the White House would 'smell like curry' if she won.

Loomer, like Harp, has travelled with Trump on his private plane.

Of course, there are the lesser lights that flicker only briefly in Trumpworld, such as the beauty queen manqué Katie Zacharia, who lasted just five days as White House press secretary in October.

It all gives the effect of a revolving door — not of the best and the brightest, but of those who are the most in awe of power.

Recall Trump's infamous 2016 debate against Hillary Clinton, to which he invited four women who had accused Bill Clinton of sexual misconduct.

In essence, Trump was saying: You may think I'm a New York City playboy, but I'm a serious man.

Now, it seems, we see the real Trump: a leader of the free world preoccupied with the adoration of younger women, no matter the cost to his legacy.

Trump's own staff are fed up.

'They like to say that behind every successful man is a strong woman,' a senior administration official tells the Daily Mail.

'Behind this president is a clique that turned the West Wing into a lunch table… A presidency can survive its enemies, but this one clearly cannot afford a mean-girl machine that would rather own the room than leave a legacy.'

Will Trump heed his own staff? Or will he leave a botched legacy… and a ballroom?
news.summary: It's incredible, and incredibly self-destructive, when you think about it: The candidate who in 2024 ran as a protector of women - well, it seems that version of Trump is long gone.

news.title: New election data raises an uncomfortable question for Republicans
news.text:
Former journalist and longtime investor and CEO of Willett Advisors Steven Rattner sorted through the post-mortem data of the 2026 election and found some trends that are flying under the radar in the analysis. Among the findings is one data point that is going to be a bombshell for the GOP. 

Speaking on "Morning Joe" Thursday, Rattner explained that since 1994 Republicans have largely reigned supreme. President Donald Trump and the modern GOP helped change that. The majority that was won on Nov. 3 is the second highest for Democrats in the post-Watergate era. 

But the more meaningful data point is what happened to Trump's MAGA base: They didn't show up. 

"About 25 million 2024 Trump voters didn't vote in a midterm House race," Rattner said on X, posting the chart. There were "3.6 million [who] backed a Democrat."

Rattner said that it isn't merely an election decided by those who showed up, but also by those who didn't. 

"So, if you take the [Kamala] Harris voters, 75 million of them back two years ago, all of these folks voted for Democrats. Virtually none of them voted for Republicans, but a hunk of them stayed home. When you look, and this is typical, of course, in midterms, when you look at Trump voters, you can see, again, very few of them, a few more, but not a huge number defected to the Democrats."

So, Democrats had turnout that was a shift from 2022, but looked more like 2018. Meanwhile, Trump voters just didn't show up. 

While there certainly was a solid chunk of Republicans who crossed sides, a "much larger share of the trump voters stayed home, just didn't vote." However, he's comparing that to the Harris numbers, which are from a general election and generally have higher turnout. 

The Brennan Center for Justice data showed another major difference: Black voters. There was a significant decrease in the Black vote in 2022, when turnout was higher in 2018. The Black vote in 2026 was higher than anything in the past 16 years. PBS News reported that the numbers for 2026 among Black voters was so significant that it rivaled that of President Barack Obama's election in 2008. 

Youth turnout, that is voters from 18-29 was the second highest it has been in 30 years. The highest turnout for young voters happened in 2018, according to the `Center for Information Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE).

news.title: Trump's Immigration Crackdowns Helped Turn Kansas Blue
news.text:
In late September, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents swarmed southwestern Kansas, where a large immigrant population is vital to the region's massive livestock industry.

The crackdown was disruptive. Businesses closed, and workers missed shifts, according to a local public radio report. The Kansas Livestock Association said the ICE operations were "having a massive chilling effect on the legal, documented, skilled workers that put beef on the table," and warned that the "unwelcome political interference" would cause prices to rise for consumers. Local officials said they were not given advance notice of the enforcement efforts.

And perhaps the most telling comment of all came from Sen. Roger Marshall (R–Kan.), a Republican lawmaker from a state that President Donald Trump had easily won in 2024.

Rather than cheering on the ICE crackdown, however, Marshall put out an official statement highlighting the "mass disruptions to local communities and businesses" and urging the Department of Homeland Security to be more "responsible" about immigration enforcement.

Marshall lost his Senate seat in November's midterm election, as Kansas elected a Democratic senator, Adam Hamilton, for the first time since 1932. The ICE raids in southwest Kansas during the closing weeks of the campaign may have played a major role in that result.

Take a look at the county-by-county results from the Kansas Senate race.

The blue areas on the state's eastern edge are usually that way—even when Trump won the state by 16 points in 2024, Kamala Harris carried the counties around Kansas City and Wichita.

What stands out on the Senate map are those blue blocks in the southwestern corner of Kansas. Hamilton won Finney, Ford, and Seward counties. That is not supposed to happen. Trump carried Finney County by 35 points in 2024, and he won the other two by even larger margins.

But that is the exact part of the state where the September immigration crackdown occurred. Dodge City, the center of the state's livestock and beef industries, is the county seat of Ford County, where voters swung by 39 points toward Hamilton.

Across Kansas, voters swung 22 points toward Democrats compared with the 2024 election, The New York Times reports. In Seward County, the swing was a staggering 52 points.

As election guru Dave Wasserman notes, Trump netted about 8,700 votes from that part of the state in 2024. Marshall, the incumbent Republican senator, lost the same region by a gap of about 900 votes. Hamilton won the election by more than 50,000 votes, so those counties were not decisive—but the results are dramatic and certainly "sums up," as Wasserman puts it, how Republicans lost the midterm.

"I'm very proud and honored that so many of the people out there voted for me," Hamilton told The Topeka Capital-Journal. "I think what they knew, they'd been hurt by the present administration and even Republicans, state legislators from that part of the state, reached out to the president and said, 'this is not OK.'"

That seems to be the message voters sent, but so far it is unclear whether the president is listening.

In an interview with 60 Minutes that aired on Sunday, Trump seemed to acknowledge that his immigration enforcement policies had gone too far.

"I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out," Trump told Ross Douthat in that interview. "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs." Later, Trump admitted more straightforwardly that his immigration policy "might be too tough."

But that conclusion is in tension with the only significant change Trump has made to his administration since the midterm drubbing. Last week, Trump announced that Stephen Miller, widely regarded as the architect of the administration's aggressive deportation policies, would be promoted to White House chief of staff.

The backlash against Trump's immigration policies goes beyond Kansas, of course. In a CBS News exit poll last week, 58 percent of voters said immigration enforcement had "gone too far."

But what happened in southwestern Kansas is particularly telling. After seeing the reality of Trump's ICE policies up close, even some of America's deepest red counties turned blue.
news.summary: Stephen Miller, the architect of Trump's immigration policies, was promoted despite the midterm losses and Trump's admission that ICE has been too harsh.
