news.title: Alex Karp Wants to Be Friends With Democrats Again
news.text:
The surveillance tech giant Palantir’s products have always been “essentially progressive,” its founder Alex Karp said Wednesday. 

Karp’s company won hundreds of millions of dollars in contracts under Donald Trump’s second term, soaring past the billion-dollar quarterly revenue mark by working with ICE to track and monitor immigrants and building AI systems for the US military. Karp has been known to praise Trump’s entrepreneurial instincts and crow about how Palantir’s technology “disrupts humanities-trained, largely Democratic voters, and makes their economic power less”—instead, empowering men in the trades. But in a Politico Playbook interview today, he appeared to change his tune, pitching himself as the right weapons-tech oligarch to surf the blue wave.

“I’ve been a Democrat my whole life,” Karp said. “I grew up in a far-left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive.”

It is true that Karp has traditionally supported Democrats—he backed Kamala Harris in 2024. But under Trump’s second term, Karp quickly allied himself with the “anti-woke” right, and profited immensely by doing so. 

Military contracting has always been a bipartisan business. But the Silicon Valley contractors who surged to power under Trump—Karp and Peter Thiel, as well as Elon Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey—haven’t been shy about declaring their allegiances with the president’s party. 

But now they’re nervous. The $1.5 trillion defense budget proposed by Pete Hegseth may be cut down in the 120th Congress. “A $1.1 trillion dollar budget will require them to make some trade-offs,” as government budget expert Mark Cancian of the Center for Strategic and International Studies put it in an article published Monday on the “tough choices, uncertainty, and scrutiny” defense contractors may now face: Companies could also be inundated with anti-corruption inquiries come January. 

Karp’s pivot is emblematic of an industry positioning itself to stay in power, no matter which party controls the government. I spoke to defense and security reporter Sharon Weinberger, whose new book, Valley of Death, tracks the rise of the “arsenal of the broligarchy,” about what we can expect from Silicon Valley’s armorers as electoral power shifts in America. 

This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

So, this assertion by Alex Karp that Palantir’s products are now “essentially progressive”—what do you make of that? 

It’s not at all surprising for me, both for Palantir and probably what you’re going to see out of other companies going forward. Palantir, even going back to its early days, has tried to thread the needle on politics, so they have both portrayed themselves as an all-seeing surveillance system—in the sense that they’re named after palantiri, these all-seeing stones that actually have ominous connotations—but at the same time, since pretty early on, they have made this argument that they themselves are not actually a surveillance system, because they are not collecting the data, but allowing the data to be integrated. 

I don’t take a side in that debate. I just think it’s very interesting that they want to portray themselves as all-powerful, but at the same time they don’t want to be portrayed as a surveillance system that violates privacy. And they’ve tried under every administration, under different eras, like the post-Snowden concerns about privacy and surveillance, to kind of have it, I would say, both ways.

Alex Karp is always a bit of a chameleon. He’s also a master of narrative. He has long identified as a Democrat, and if you look at his political donations, he—like other people involved in defense—actually kind of sprinkles the money around, because they have to survive in both Democratic and Republican administrations. 

But he was always positioning himself ultimately as a Democrat for a long time, up until December 2024, at the Reagan National Defense Forum, which is the major bipartisan defense forum that’s held every year at the Reagan Library in California. He gets up as part of his panel, as part of his talk, and starts blasting the Democrats for their, quote, “woke pagan ideology.” It was sort of unprecedented for the CEO of a major defense contractor to attack a political party, either political party.

Given that, do you expect the results of last week’s midterms to affect the “arsenal of the broligarchy” that you write about?

What I’ve long argued is that people have real beliefs. I don’t doubt that Alex Karp has real beliefs. Peter Thiel certainly has real beliefs about the Antichrist and many other things. 

But as companies, they have to survive in Democratic and Republican administrations, and they’re going to do that by maneuvering in their language and their narrative. They’re going to do that by the people they hire, which will be from both administrations, and the lobbyists they hire. But what is so different and a little bit dangerous about some of these new wave of defense companies like Palantir is that they have broken the norms of being bipartisan, where defense has long been a bipartisan issue. 

So it’s not just whether they go from Democrat to Republican. And another pivot that’s worth mentioning—in fact, it’s I would say it’s a triple pivot for Karp—in the book, I have this picture of him in his Haverford College yearbook photo, draped in a keffiyeh. 

I was going to ask you about the keffiyeh photo!

Karp may be just a little bit older than me. I don’t believe the same things I believed 20 or 30 years ago. I don’t criticize him personally for going through a political transformation, but after the October 7 attacks and then the expansion of the war in Gaza, he became a very vocal critic of some of the college campus protests.

That gives me pause for two reasons. We don’t really want the heads of our defense contractors to be commenting on domestic political speech. It’s a norm issue, not whether I agree or disagree with what he is saying, but also it reflects this amazing chameleon-like transformation that he’s made. And he’s making it again, if you look at some of his most recent remarks, because after October 7, it was “we stand with Israel.” 

Now in some recent remarks, he’s a little bit backing away from that, just as you’re seeing with his remarks on ICE and immigration about going too far. The guy is a master of narrative. I give him credit on that. My biggest problem is not what he believes or doesn’t believe, but the way that we have traditionally expected our defense companies to stay out of politics. 

Another major Silicon Valley contractor that I have on the mind right now is Elon Musk, who spent something like $400 million supporting losing candidates in the midterms. Do you expect to see any kind of similar pivot now from him?

Musk is the more extreme case. My issues with Musk are not his personal views or his political views, but again, the norm-breaking. He’s going to have a tougher time clawing back. But he’s also in a little bit of a different position because SpaceX has a de facto monopoly on military space launch. 

That being said, business-wise, he’s not suicidal. I think it’ll be really interesting to watch what he does. He has certainly been influenced by the fact that Tesla has connections in China, and he has always backed away from making major criticisms of China. I suspect he will learn to like, if not love, a Democratic Congress.

This also depends on what happens with the next administration in two years. I suspect that we are also going to see some—I don’t know if moderation is the right word—but I wouldn’t be surprised if he shifts, if not his political position, then certainly his involvement in politics. I would not be surprised at all.

I think what he’ll see is that his dalliances, both with DOGE and his very right-wing stance, could be a detriment to his business. And I think he cares about his business above anything else. I’m not sure that he’s going to go and start embracing Democrats right away. But I do think that he is not going to try to fight a prevailing administration or Congress.

Any chance we’ll see a Silicon Valley version of the 1993 Pentagon Last Supper, when the Department of Defense warned weapons-makers that the government’s weapons-buying budget would shrink? 

I mean, when the stock market bubble eventually collapses—we now have dozens, if not hundreds, of startups—you will see consolidation. Venture capitalists will tell you this. There is going to be a vast consolidation of these new startups, but that’s separate from the politics. Elon Musk has really notched successes with SpaceX in space launch, but the others have not proved themselves. 

The question I raise is, if Silicon Valley companies become the new prime [contractors], are they going to be any better, faster, cheaper, or more innovative than the old primes?

news.title: Economic Populism Lost, Again
news.text: It’s frankly eerie how much Trump’s playbook over the past year mirrored Biden’s before it—in both form and electoral result. The Biden administration, you may recall, spent its early days “going big” with a convoluted, deficit-busting $1.9 trillion fiscal stimulus, while Trump “went big” with the convoluted, deficit-busting One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Both pushed industrial policies—subsidies, tariffs, “Buy American” rules, and more—that raised consumer prices, increased bureaucracy, and rewarded political allies. Team Biden also brushed off inflation as “transitory” and then pivoted to bragging about disinflation (inflation growing more slowly) and GDP growth. As noted above, Trump did much the same. And Biden campaigned in 2024 at various subsidized/protected factory sites, championing “Bidenomics” to inflation-weary voters who weren’t interested in what he and Kamala Harris were selling. In 2026, the same voters got the “Trumponomics” version, and they issued the same judgment.
news.summary: Voters again rejected the price-hiking agenda that both parties have spent a decade selling them.

news.title: CNN Data Guru Reveals Voter Group That ‘Despises’ President
news.text:
CNN data analyst Harry Enten has revealed that young voter support for President Donald Trump is cratering. 

On Thursday, CNN’s Kate Bolduan discussed new midterm data with Enten, who said it showed an astonishing collapse in support for the president among voters aged 18-24. 

“Look at this margin. Look at this margin. That is wild. Yeah, it’s huge. It’s a huge shift. I mean, that is like this isn’t over 20 years. This is over two years,” said Enten, pointing to election data showing that Trump’s net approval by younger voters had fallen from 43 percent in 2024 to just 15 percent this year. 

“We are talking about a 28-point decline in terms of where he went from vote share to approval rating in just two years’ time,” said Enten. “This drove a historic shift away from the Republicans to the Democrats.”

“They, simply put, despised the president of the United States,” he said.

news.title: Colombia’s FM apologizes to Democrats for past social media comments
news.text:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula has issued a public apology to members of the United States Democratic Party over a series of offensive comments he previously made on social media, in a diplomatic effort to distance the government of President Abelardo de la Espriella from his past political rhetoric.

In a letter dated November 10 and made public on Wednesday, November 11, Bula acknowledged that his earlier remarks about Democratic leaders, including Kamala Harris, Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton, had been inappropriate and disrespectful. The apology comes just days after Democrats secured a sweeping victory in the November 3 US midterm elections, winning control of both chambers of Congress and several governorships.

“I want to offer my sincere apologies for comments I made in past social media posts about leaders of the Democratic Party. The language I used was inappropriate and disrespectful, and I regret the words and the offence they caused,” Bula wrote.

The foreign minister was responding to renewed scrutiny of posts published before his appointment to Colombia’s diplomatic service. Bula sought to make clear that his previous statements belonged to a different political moment and should not be interpreted as an indication of the current administration’s diplomatic priorities.

“Those posts were written long before I became Minister of Foreign Affairs, in the context of a particular presidential election. While that context helps explain the circumstances in which they were made, it does not diminish my responsibility for what I wrote,” he acknowledged.

“My perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they in any way represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

The timing of the apology is politically significant. The Democratic victory in the midterms has transformed the balance of power in Washington, ending unified Republican control of Congress and placing the party in a position to exercise considerably greater influence over legislation, government spending and congressional oversight.

For Colombia, the implications extend well beyond the domestic politics of the United States. Washington remains one of Bogotá’s most important strategic partners, with bilateral cooperation spanning security, intelligence sharing, counternarcotics operations, trade, investment and regional stability.

The relationship has historically enjoyed bipartisan support in the United States, surviving changes of government in both countries. From the implementation of Plan Colombia to subsequent security and economic cooperation agreements, successive Democratic and Republican administrations have recognized the importance of maintaining a close relationship with Bogotá.

That institutional continuity is particularly important for a Colombian government seeking to consolidate its relationship with Washington. While President De la Espriella has aligned his administration with Donald Trump’s Republican leadership on security and regional policy, the Democrats’ congressional gains mean that Colombia cannot afford to approach its relationship with the United States exclusively through a Republican political lens.

Congress has an important role in determining foreign assistance, approving budgets and overseeing international security programmes. Consequently, maintaining constructive relations with Democratic lawmakers will be essential to safeguarding the continuity of programmes that have underpinned bilateral cooperation for decades.

Bula’s letter appears designed to address precisely the current realpolitik.

Since taking office, the Foreign Minister says he has advocated a bipartisan approach to Colombia’s relationship with the United States. He also emphasized that the country’s interests must take precedence over individual political affiliations.

“As Minister of Foreign Affairs, I have a responsibility to represent Colombia with respect, openness and a commitment to constructive dialogue,” he wrote, adding that this responsibility requires listening to different perspectives and advancing the shared interests of both countries.

The message was also intended to demonstrate that Bogotá recognizes the importance of maintaining relationships across the American political spectrum, regardless of electoral cycles or differences between the two parties.

Bula’s apology follows criticism from Democratic lawmakers, including Representative Gregory Meeks, who raised concerns about the minister’s previous statements and called on the De la Espriella administration to address the issue.

The diplomatic challenge is therefore not simply one of managing an uncomfortable social media history. It is about establishing the credibility of Colombia’s foreign policy at a moment when the political landscape in Washington has shifted considerably.

For a country whose security and economic interests remain closely connected to the United States, the ability to work with both Republicans and Democrats is a strategic necessity rather than a diplomatic courtesy.

Bula has acknowledged that his impetuous language was inappropriate. Whether his apology is sufficient to restore confidence among Democratic lawmakers remains to be seen. But his message is clear: the foreign policy of Colombia must be measured by the interests and priorities of the country, not by the political opinions its foreign minister expressed before assuming office.

The diplomatic outreach was also reflected in Bogotá’s relationship with another longstanding North American partner. On November 11, Bula met with Canada’s Vice Minister of International Development, Cynthia Termorshuizen, to reaffirm more than seven decades of diplomatic relations between the two countries and explore opportunities to deepen their strategic partnership.

The discussions focused on expanding cooperation in agriculture, strengthening micro, small and medium-sized businesses, supporting rural entrepreneurship and training, and promoting development projects led by women. Both delegations also identified opportunities for investment in clean energy, agro-industry, infrastructure and responsible mining, with an emphasis on sustainable economic growth and regional development.

Colombia’s Foreign Ministry said the objective was to continue consolidating the country as a key Canadian partner in Latin America, generating opportunities and well-being across both nations.

Taken together, Bula’s diplomatic engagements underline the importance of a foreign policy built around institutional relationships and economic cooperation. Whether dealing with Republicans and Democrats in Washington or strengthening longstanding partnerships with Ottawa, Colombia’s interests ultimately depend on its ability to maintain constructive relations across political divides.

news.title: The Greatest Ever Political Ad That Helped Scott Colom Win Mississippi
news.text: The greatest political advertisement of all time? It might just be. Democrat Scott Colom’s “pick another protein” ad is being hailed as one of the most brilliant spots ever created for a political campaign, receiving credit for his stunning triumph over Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi’s closely contested Senate race. Colom’s win, which further pads Democrats' Senate majority, is a monumental shift for a state that has been controlled by white conservatives for generations. The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and Colom, a local prosecutor, is the state’s first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction. “All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” he told supporters at his victory rally on Wednesday night. “I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters.” He spoke behind a sign that said "Picked Another Senator," a reference to the hugely successful ad. Democratic Party leaders have hailed Colom’s victory, with Senator Chuck Schumer saying Colom “ran the campaign of a lifetime and re-imagined what’s possible for Democrats in the South.” He "proved the polls, the pundits, and the prognosticators wrong at every turn," Schumer wrote on X. Few had predicted the race would even be competitive, with polls and forecasters favoring Hyde-Smith. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rated the race as “solid Republican” for much of the cycle before adjusting to “likely Republican” in late October. But while Schumer thought Mississippi could be in play this year, his Senate Majority PAC didn't pour money into the race until the final stretch, long after Black Democrats led by Representative Bennie Thompson of Mississippi had urged party leaders and donors to view the deep-red state as winnable and invest in the race. The race drew national attention only after Colom released a slick and funny ad in mid-October that honed in on the affordability crisis, an issue that brought down Republicans across the map in the midterms. The 28-second spot revived comments Hyde-Smith made earlier this year, where she dismissed high beef prices by saying Mississippians have “so many proteins to choose from.” In the ad, several incredulous Mississippians firmly reject the idea of picking another protein, telling the camera they’d rather “pick another senator instead.” The ad went massively viral, with one man’s delivery of a line in a distinctly Southern drawl becoming a particularly iconic moment. “Pick another protein? Sheee-it, I’d rather pick another senator instead,” he says. ‘Centering The Voters’ Ryan Sayles, who directed and edited the ad, said he brought “Mississippi culture” to the spot, referencing that line in particular. “Shooting the video, he was like, ‘Pick another protein? S***, I’d rather pick another senator,’” Sayles told Crooked Media. “I was like, ‘no no no, we gotta drag that part out.’” Russ Hudson, the Army veteran who took on the role after his father balked at having to utter an expletive on camera, told The New York Times that he delivered the line “like a Mississippian would.” He’s now become an unexpected sensation in the state, and says he is regularly stopped and asked to repeat the line. Sayles, who said Colom’s campaign is the first he’s worked on, attributed the ad’s success largely to how it focused on voters and the issues that matter to them. That’s something Colom did throughout the campaign, he said. "I think the biggest thing was centering the voters, letting them say how they feel, and I think that's why it worked so well,” Sayles said. “If you really look at it, Scott was in the ad for about five seconds, and that's our biggest ad…. because it really wasn't about him, it was about Mississippi. And I think that was what made that ad so powerful. It was just like, you're really capturing how people are feeling right now.” Newsweek has contacted Sayles for further comment via social media. The day after Election Day, Colom credited the ad as a game-changing moment for his campaign, and said Sayles should be considered “the break-out star of this cycle.” The Mississippi race was not considered a must-win for Democrats to retake control of the Senate, and it wasn't until the final stretch of the cycle that Democrats began efforts to boost Colom in earnest. Not long after the ad debuted, Senate Majority PAC, the super political action committee aimed at boosting Democratic Senate candidates, announced it would launch a $1.2 million ad campaign in the race. The super PAC later invested another $1 million. “It is clear Colom is running a competitive race that has put Hyde-Smith on her heels,” the PAC’s spokesperson Lauren French told The Hill at the time. Former President Barack Obama endorsed Colom in a campaign ad on October 12. Ten days later, former Vice President Kamala Harris rallied with Colom at a high school. And in a sign that Republicans were wary of losses even in deep-red states, President Donald Trump made a late-October stop in Mississippi to stump for Hyde-Smith. "I'm here because Cindy's doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can't take a chance," Trump told the crowd at the rally on October 26. ‘Moved The Needle’ For some, Colom’s “pick another protein” ad is the best of the midterms cycle, if not all time. "If he wins, this has to go down as one of the best political ads of all time,” political forecaster Nate Silver wrote on X before the race was called. After Colom's win, progressive YouTuber Jack Cocchiarella said it is “officially the greatest political ad in American history.” Political experts told Newsweek that it's difficult to assess the impact of any particular ad on a race, but that in a close contest, anything that causes even a small shift in voter sentiment can prove consequential. "No doubt its virality helped move the needle with some voters, and in a race this close, it only takes a little movement to make a difference," Marvin King, an associate professor at the University of Mississippi who focuses on African American politics, told Newsweek. Alex Coppock, an associate professor of political science at Northwestern University who has researched the impact of digital advertising on voter turnout, said the ad likely reached more voters than others. "The ad is funny, uses profanity in an authentic way, has memorable alliteration and wordplay, so I bet that it garnered above average attention," Coppock told Newsweek. "This ad might have made a difference in such an extremely tight race, especially if it reached many people and stuck in their minds because it was so clever,” he said. Brian Shoup, a professor of political science at Mississippi State University, told Newsweek that the ad "helped nationalize this race in a way that brought significant viral attention to Colom's campaign.” He said: "Prior to the fall, Colom's campaign wasn't receiving as much support from Democratic-aligned PACs and organizations, something that Mississippi Democratic leaders have long complained about. ”The ad, by going viral, definitely helped his campaign attract more financial support." Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick and Emma Lee-Sang
news.summary: Colom's viral ad is being hailed as one of the most brilliant ads ever after his historic victory in Mississippi's Senate race.

news.title: Biden: Had I Known About the Cancer, I Would Have Quit the Race
news.text:
Former U.S. President Joe Biden has said he would have abandoned his re-election bid had he known he was suffering from cancer, in a rare interview with People magazine published Wednesday, a week before the release of his memoir, Promise Me, America.

Biden, who stepped aside in the final stretch of the 2024 campaign to make way for Kamala Harris, addressed the July debate against Donald Trump that first triggered alarm over his fitness for office. The then-president appeared confused during the exchange, searching for words and at times seeming disoriented. According to CNN, his wife, Jill Biden, feared he was having a stroke.

“A Mistake,” But Not Decisive

Biden dismissed the debate as a minor episode, calling it “a mistake” and playing down its impact on a campaign that ended with Trump’s return to power and defeat for the Democrats.

“To me, it wasn’t very important. I figured there would be another debate. But even without another one, it didn’t throw me, because it wasn’t decisive,” he said.

In the wide-ranging interview, Biden conceded a single regret: that he would not have run for a second term had he known he was ill.

“If I had known I felt this bad because I had cancer, I would have resigned. I wouldn’t have run, because I don’t think an 80-year-old man with cancer should seek the presidency,” he said.

Diagnosis Disclosed After Leaving Office

Biden insisted he never sought to conceal his condition and announced the illness “as soon as he knew what was happening.” The disclosure came in May 2025, 118 days after the end of his term, People noted.

Asked whether he regretted handing the nomination to Harris just three months before Election Day, Biden was unequivocal: “I think objectively, I was the person best qualified to hold that office.”

The rest is history: after a hastily assembled campaign, the Democrat failed to win over voters, who preferred Trump.

news.title: 4 Potential 2028 Presidential Contenders Stand Out In New Poll
news.text:
WASHINGTON, Nov 12 (Reuters) - Four potential contenders in the 2028 race for the White House have caught American voters’ attention with their early jockeying: Republicans JD Vance and Marco Rubio and Democrats Jon Ossoff and Pete Buttigieg, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll.

None of the four has yet formally launched a campaign and the parties’ 2028 nominating contests are more than a year away, leaving plenty of time for new contenders to emerge and for voters’ views to change.

Some 45% of Republican voters polled said they believed Secretary of State Rubio would be an “excellent” presidential candidate, with 43% saying the same of Vice President Vance. Former Transportation Secretary Buttigieg and US Senator Ossoff, of Georgia, each got that rating from 29% of Democratic voters.

The poll, which surveyed 1,705 US adults nationwide including roughly 500 registered voters from each party and was completed on Monday, had a margin of error of 5 percentage points for Republican and Democratic voters.

President Donald Trump, struggling with an approval rating near the lowest of his career, looms large over the conversation for both parties. Republicans are divided on whether they want a candidate who breaks with Trump or follows in his footsteps, while Democrats, who are flying high after routing Republicans in the November 3 congressional elections, are divided on how aggressively to go after the president, such as through impeachment.

Trump has quizzed allies on whom they prefer Vance or Rubio and in a Sunday interview with CBS’s “60 Minutes” said he would “not necessarily” make an endorsement in the Republican primary.

‘MANAGED TO DO HIS JOB’

Barbara Rezner, an attorney in Florida who voted for Trump in the last three presidential elections, said she prefers Rubio over Vance, whom she considers too far to the right and too close to the president.

“Rubio has managed to do his job. He’s stayed off most people’s radar because he hasn’t done anything too far left, too far right, too crazy,” Rezner said.

The modest but growing dissatisfaction with Trump among Republicans is centered on the president’s decision to launch a war on Iran that has driven fuel prices higher. Rubio has been notably absent from many of the so-far fruitless peace talks with Iran despite being the nation’s top diplomat. Vance has shown signs of wanting to distance himself as well, saying publicly that the Republican drubbing in the midterm elections owed to the war with Iran.

A dozen-odd other Republicans are also in the national conversation over 2028 contenders, with Florida Governor Ron DeSantis among the best regarded, with 32% of Republicans rating him as an excellent option. Others - like Trump’s son, Donald Trump Jr., and Texas US Senator Ted Cruz - have their fans, but also many detractors.

OSSOFF AND BUTTIGIEG

Among Democrats, Ossoff is at the top of many voters’ lists, with 29% of the party’s registered voters rating him as excellent. Ossoff has grabbed headlines in recent months by calling Trump corrupt and unfit for office in unusually direct language, and last week he won his re-election race by 18 percentage points in Georgia, a state Trump carried by 2 points in 2024.

Buttigieg also gets the excellent rating from 29% of Democrats. Buttigieg also ran for president in 2020 and is better known nationally than Ossoff.

About one in five Democrats say they have never heard of Buttigieg, compared to roughly one in three who say the same about Ossoff. Very few Republicans are unfamiliar with Vance, but about one in six said they do not know who Rubio is. For candidates in either party, starting the election cycle with more name recognition can save money that would be spent getting the candidate’s name out, but examples abound of little-known candidates catching fire during the campaign, as happened with former President Bill Clinton.

Buttigieg and Ossoff are considered moderates among Democrats, and that appeals to Democratic voters like Ed Blair, a retired pig farmer in southern Illinois, who gives Buttigieg a better rating in part because Ossoff is less familiar.

“I do favor the more moderate candidates over the more progressive ones,” said Blair, who is wary of proposed major shifts like expanding federal Medicare health insurance coverage from all seniors to everyone in the country. Blair would prefer gradual shifts, such as expanding Medicare to cover all children. “In going towards some of the progressive policies, small steps need to be taken rather than large ones to give people time to adapt.”

The Reuters/Ipsos poll shows other well-known moderates - like former Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost to Trump in the 2024 presidential election, and California Governor Gavin Newsom - each get “excellent candidate” ratings of 23%, higher than the 15% of Democrats who view progressive stalwart Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a US representative for New York, that way.

Ocasio-Cortez told CNN after the midterms that impeaching Trump should be an option on the table, while Buttigieg told the New Yorker magazine he is “not very interested” in impeachment.

Elaine Kamarck, a Democratic strategist, cautioned against reading too deeply into the public’s current views this far out from the 2028 election. “It’s a world away,” Kamarck said. “There are lots of people in both parties who are still deciding if they are going to run. You might be able to predict who will run, but you certainly don’t know anything about who is going to be ahead.”

news.title: The Candidates Who Defeated the Politics of White Grievance
news.text:
Apparently, there is an expiration date on the red-meat racism of Trumpism. El-Sayed defeated his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, by seven points. Elsewhere, Republicans attempted to link Black candidates to chaos and crime, but these tried-and-true tactics appear to have had little effect. Angie Nixon, a Florida state representative and union organizer, ran an upstart campaign for the U.S. Senate, and was subject to witheringly racist attacks from the President and his supporters. Laura Loomer, who boasts of her access to Trump, described Nixon as “a ghetto, black, communist.” She mocked Nixon’s speech as “Ebonics” and wrote, “Maybe I need to bark at you and tug your leash and then you’ll finally understand.” Trump said of Nixon, “She’s not of the intellect that should be running for the Senate. She’s a very-low-I.Q. person.” Yet Nixon—who ran a campaign centered on Medicare for All, universal child care, and taxing billionaires—came within three points of defeating the Republican incumbent, Ashley Moody, converting an estimated six per cent of Floridians who voted for Trump in 2024.
In the Georgia gubernatorial race, the Democratic candidate, Keisha Lance Bottoms, was pitted against the Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire health-care executive who spent more than two hundred million dollars of his own money on the election. Bottoms, who served as the mayor of Atlanta during Trump’s first term, gained prominence during those years as one of the President’s opponents: she denied ICE the right to hold detainees in the city’s jail, in response to the Administration’s family-detention practices, and opposed the rapid reopening of Georgia at the height of the pandemic. Jackson, a white man, repeatedly blamed Bottoms for violent crime in Atlanta and for the 2020 unrest in response to police brutality—often conflating the two. Not to be outdone, Trump held a rally outside of Macon, where he accused Bottoms of having “destroyed Atlanta with her crime and filth and constant riots.” She won the race by nearly nine percentage points, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of any state. Across Georgia, seven other Black women won statewide seats.
In Louisiana, Jamie Davis, a third-generation Black farmer, ran for the Senate on what he called the “four pillars” of affordability, education, health care, and upholding the Constitution. He also supported a moratorium on building new data centers and pledged to introduce legislation barring elected officials from signing nondisclosure agreements. According to a local news investigation, his opponent, Representative Julia Letlow, signed an N.D.A. with Meta about a fifty-billion-dollar data-center project in her district; she went on to purchase stock in Meta and then failed to disclose those trades for more than a year, in violation of federal law. (In response to the reporting, a spokesperson for Letlow said that these purchases were made by a broker and that she did not direct any of her trades.)
Astonishingly, Davis was neck and neck with Letlow well into the fall, when, in an act of desperation, a Republican PAC released an ad showing an A.I.-generated Davis lumbering toward the camera in a T-shirt and jeans. A Louisiana Republican pollster, Bernie Pinsonat, explained to a local Fox News affiliate that the ad was intended “to turn any whites off that would think about voting for him. You know, we do have a lot of RINOs”—Republicans in Name Only—“in this state.” Davis came within two points of Letlow, losing by a mere twenty-five thousand votes. The Fox News Voter Poll for Louisiana estimates that he earned the support of ninety-two per cent of Black voters, thirty-four per cent of white voters, and eleven per cent of people who said they had voted for Trump in 2024. Every parish shifted toward Democrats by at least nine points.
The outcome may well have been different had Davis received meaningful assistance from the national Democratic Party. Days before the election, the longtime Democratic Party consultant and Louisiana native son James Carville noted, “I beat my head against the wall trying to get some national money in here. It’s almost impossible.” Scott Colom, the Democratic Senate candidate in Mississippi, whose exceedingly close race was called in his favor on Wednesday, was also left out in the cold. In July, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee made a forty-million-dollar investment in ten Senate battlegrounds, part of which funded outreach to Black voters, that did not include Mississippi—even though a poll had shown that Colom was within three points of the Republican incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith. Finally, the D.S.C.C. joined Colom on a five-hundred-thousand-dollar ad buy with just six days left to vote.
The G.O.P.’s racist attacks may not have worked to turn out white voters, but they undoubtedly helped to mobilize Black voters. These date back to the Administration’s war on D.E.I.—specifically, its attack on Black workers in the federal government, led by Elon Musk and the short-lived DOGE. By September, 2026, federal employment had fallen by roughly three hundred and twenty-eight thousand jobs since Trump took office. Multiple lawsuits have alleged that the firings targeted Black workers, who made up roughly eighteen per cent of the federal workforce in 2024. (The Trump Administration has responded that its firings were not racially biased.) The attacks on Black employment were amplified by the continued evisceration of the Voting Rights Act. After the Supreme Court’s Callais decision, in April—which allowed states to redraw, or “crack,” districts that concentrated Black voters to assure their representation—Louisiana dismantled its second majority-Black congressional district, Tennessee split Memphis’s Black communities among three districts, and Alabama reinstated a map that reduced Black voters’ share of the voting-age population in its Second Congressional District.
Just two years ago, Republicans boasted about their new currency with Black men and Latino voters. But the A.P. Voter Poll estimates that, this year, about ninety per cent of Black voters supported Democratic House candidates; roughly eighty per cent backed Kamala Harris in 2024. Only about ten per cent of Black male voters supported Republican candidates, just two years after approximately twenty-five per cent cast ballots for Trump. In Louisiana, where the Callais case originated, Black voters cast more than eighty-six thousand early and absentee ballots—an eighty-three-per-cent increase from the 2022 midterms.
In Alabama, Representative Shomari Figures, a Democrat, won reëlection in the cracked Second Congressional District by nearly eight points. The candidates in Louisiana’s cracked Sixth District are headed to a runoff election. In Tennessee, the Democratic state representative Justin J. Pearson ran in a newly configured district, which previously was centered on Memphis and now stretches over roughly two hundred miles, only to lose by some twenty-five hundred votes to his Republican opponent. In fourteen of the fifteen counties making up the new seat, Republican majorities voted for Trump in the 2024 election. Across these counties, Pearson won 48.5 per cent of the vote.
Pearson is a longtime progressive activist, but not all of these candidates are on the left—Davis ran as a gun-toting farmer and business owner. Nearly all of them, however, campaigned on the affordability crisis, which extends far beyond the cost of gas. Their campaigns upend the assumption of many Democratic consultants that rural and Southern outposts are a poor use of financial resources and political talent. Whether they mark a political turning point will depend upon whether Democrats now choose to take the whole of America, and especially the South, seriously. If Party leaders invest in the Southern candidates who are attracting Black, white, and brown voters and rebuilding regional political organizations, they may find the source of a sustained electoral turnaround. If they do not, we can expect right-wing forces to reassemble a possibly more dangerous version of Trumpism—more serious, more determined, and more destructive. ♦
news.summary: Will Democrats’ breakthrough in the South transform their party’s view of a winning campaign?

news.title: Alex Karp Said He’s a ‘Progressive.’ OK! Here’s Some Other Stuff He’s Said Recently
news.text:
“I’ve been a Democrat my whole life,” Karp told Politico, which noted that he called the Democratic Party “totally irresponsible” in the distant time of October 2025. “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive.”
This isn’t the first time Karp has called himself a progressive. In 2018, The New York Times reported that Karp described himself as such. In the same article, he claimed to have voted for Hillary Clinton.
Karp has also donated money to Democratic candidates. In 2023, for instance, he donated $360,000 to a joint fundraising committee for Joe Biden and Kamala Harris. The next year, he donated $1 million to MAGA, Inc.
Palantir has a share of supporters from the Democratic party. However, it’s not necessarily clear how the products of Palantir—a company that built the technology that underpins much of the Trump administration's brutal arrest and deportation campaign, sold tools to the US military that can use generative AI to help plan and execute drone strikes, and partnered with the Israeli military to assist in its devastating war on the Gaza strip, among other things—could reasonably be seen as progressive.
It’s instructive, then, to look at what else Karp has said in recent weeks, and how it lines up with his idea of what’s “progressive.”
In his most recent quarterly letter to Palantir shareholders, Karp actually doubled down on his basic premise. In it, he argued that Palantir employees are “the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement.”
“We are all, in no uncertain terms, living through what John Lewis Gaddis, the professor of naval and military history at Yale, presciently described decades ago as the long peace,” Karp wrote, despite the fact that the US and Iran are currently engaged in direct warfare.
During Palantir’s corresponding earnings call on November 2, Karp was asked to clarify the statements in his letter.
“Our products are built to avoid war, meaning the adversary knows that they will have such pain inflicted upon them that in fact it's not worth going to war,” Karp said. He did not, however, address the relevant possibility that the US is the party that initiates war.
“I grew up as a lefty,” Karp continued. “I don't actually like war. I want to avoid war. I don't support wars.” But he said, “Sometimes they are necessary, and when they are necessary, America and its allies need the very, very, very best tools.”
Karp went on to say that Palantir has both a “moral imperative” and a “mission reason” for having the “somewhat crazy aspiration” of dominating its market. That mission, Karp said, is supporting the war fighter. Conveniently, it’s also very profitable.
“We are delighted that we can support the war fighter even more because we're making so much money,” Karp said.
Karp’s recent comments in Politico could also be seen through the lens of convenience. Democrats will have a majority in both chambers of Congress next year, and since about half of Palantir’s revenue comes from government work, it’s pragmatic to sow goodwill. Palantir has seen continued success, after all, across Democratic and Republican administrations.
However, Karp doesn’t care about cultivating favor with everybody. He pointedly excludes anyone who has criticized Palantir in what he calls “ridiculously stupid and malicious, incredibly hard to understand attacks.” (Karp didn’t name examples, although many critiques of Palantir have come from the American left.)
“What motivates me is helping to make sure we are fighting for you,” Karp said, addressing Palantir investors, “and quite frankly, making sure that the people that made fun of you and made fun of us are suffering.”

news.text:

The debate over how and why Democrats won will influence what measures the new majority caucuses will take up first and how far those actions should go.

Third Way struck early, with a Nov. 4 memo that claimed "high-quality" moderate candidates "were the majority makers" in this year's midterms.

Of the 44 House seats that flipped this cycle, about 29 came from red districts that President Donald Trump won by double-digit margins in 2024. The group calculates those candidates outperformed former Vice President Kamala Harris's 2024 margin by an average of 15 percentage points in those districts.

Democrats have similarly flipped at least seven Senate seats in states the president won with contenders who've ripped the White House, but stopped short of demanding Medicare for All or abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

"That's a pretty profound answer to this question that we've long debated about whether all of the energy is on the left," DeGruyter said. "There was a hell of a lot of energy in North Carolina and Georgia and Kansas and Texas, and that is why Democrats have an incredible opportunity here to take back the middle from Trump."

Like many of the Democrats who flipped Republican seats, Hamilton − who won by 5 percentage points in Kansas, which hasn't sent a Democrat to the Senate since Franklin Delano Roosevelt was president − stressed being "independent-minded."

Hamilton, a 62-year-old Methodist pastor and former Republican, espoused views cheered by the Democratic base such as opposing tax breaks for AI data centers, expanding Medicare coverage for seniors and investigating "private equity consolidation" to break up monopolies. He also supports restoring what he called "disastrous cuts" to Medicaid through the president's "one, big beautiful" bill.

But in post-election interviews, the Kansas Democrat has already begun positioning himself as a counterweight to more liberal-minded colleagues on Medicare for All, which he said isn't the "right approach" on health care.

He attributed the decisive margin this month to a coalition of independents and previously disengaged voters, who largely backed Democrats in purple districts.

"People who have been homeless politically came in in overwhelming numbers, and not just came in for Democrats, but switched sides or came off the sidelines profoundly in this cycle," Libby said.

"I don't think this was a victory for the Democratic brand," he added. "I'm not entirely sure the Democrats have a brand right now, and I think that's something that they absolutely have to fix between now and the 2028 presidential race."

Democrats running in red states in 2026 were often difficult to pigeonhole ideologically.

Sen.-elect Josh Turek, who won in Iowa after Trump carried the state by double digits two years ago, prefers creating a public health insurance option to Medicare for All. On social issues, the two-time Paralympic gold medalist released an ad that infuriated some Iowa Democrats and trans rights supporters for opposing transgender women competing in female sports and "taxpayers paying for sex changes."

Libby points out that roughly two-thirds of self-described moderate voters supported the Democratic candidate in their local contests, up from the approximately 6 in 10 moderates who backed Harris in 2024, the Associated Press reported.

Progressives push back against centrist narrative

Progressive activists say many of the candidates being labeled "moderate" by centrist groups are better described as "outsiders." Many of those candidates running in historically Republican areas ran against corporate power and the Washington establishment of both parties.

"If those who call themselves moderate want to put their label on issues that we've (championed) and trying to make more popular for years, then great, we have consensus around our issues — that's awesome," said Adam Green, cofounder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, a left-leaning grassroots group involved in several primary contests this year.

The PCCC backed Sen.-elect James Talarico, of Texas, along with candidates such as Rep.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, one of six democratic socialists heading to Washington.

During much of the Texas Senate race, Talarico, who prevailed by 12 percentage points, railed against billionaires. He often talked about U.S. politics being more "top versus bottom" rather than left versus right.

On the senator-elect's website, Talarico said he supports making "billionaires pay their fair share in taxes, including by imposing a higher tax on their income and capital gains," which Green and others say sounds much more like Sens. Bernie Sanders, of Vermont, and Elizabeth Warren, of Massachusetts, than so-called moderate Democrats.

But Talarico also tried to back away from the progressive label as he campaigned in a state that hadn't elected a Democrat to the Senate in over 30 years. During the course of the campaign, the 37-year-old state legislator and Presbyterian seminary student said he opposed abolishing ICE and reversed course on supporting trans athletes in girls' sports.

The PCCC's sister organization, PCCC Institute, shared its "How Dems Ran" database, which examined 60 competitive midterm elections, exclusively with USA TODAY. Research examined those candidates' debates, speeches, social media content, campaign ads and websites, finding Democrats who won even in red states and districts supported many left-leaning proposals.

Roughly 98% backed a ban on stock trading by lawmakers, according to the group's research. Another 85% supported some version of expanding public health care coverage through either Medicare for All, a public option, or Medicare buy-in.

An October KFF poll showed 66% of U.S. adults favor having a national health plan, the largest total since the foundation began measuring the issue in 2017. That support includes 72% of independents and 34% of Republicans who support Medicare for All, according to the survey.

"If the corporate-aligned Democrats at Third Way want to somehow lay claim to that style of politics, we've just won the battle for this whole of the Democratic Party," Green told USA TODAY.

Some progressive candidates also won in swing states, such as Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who supports Medicare for All and ending U.S. aid to Israel. He won Michigan by 8 percentage points and has been touted by progressives as proof their movement can win, in the words of Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-New York, "anywhere."

Populists who defy center or left label

Some red-state winners, such as Rep.-elect Sam Forstag, of Montana, created a populist message that was embraced by top progressive figures from the outset of his campaign against Republican Aaron Flint to replace Ryan Zinke, a Republican who served as interior secretary in Trump's first term.

The 32-year-old union leader and political newcomer won by three percentage points in a western Montana district, which borders Idaho, that Trump won by four times as much in 2024. He was endorsed by Sanders and Ocasio-Cortez but later received support during the general election from the moderate Blue Dog Coalition.

"We don't see our, like, fundamental lived experience reflected in the people who are representing us purportedly in Congress," Forstag told USA TODAY.

He believes in expanding Medicare, raising the minimum wage to $15 an hour and banning congressional stock trading. But he also favors reforming ICE over abolishing the agency and supports protecting gun rights.

Forstag will join both the rival Blue Dogs and the Congressional Progressive Caucus.

He explained his desire to embrace populism in a social media video Nov. 9, saying both factions are needed to achieve the American people's goals.

"I will be one of just a few Democrats who are sitting in both of those caucuses," he said. "You see, the overlap is, well, giving us the chance to fight for populist economic policies that are actually going to help working people."

Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter bested scandal-ridden Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio, a Trump White House alum whose bitter divorce battle involved domestic violence allegations from Emily Moreno, the daughter of Sen. Bernie Moreno, by 10 percentage points.

Poindexter's campaign contrasted Miller's biography with the union ironworker’s rugged image. He is counted among the flips by centrist groups, but progressives point out that he called for ending tax breaks for the wealthy, banning dark money spending in campaigns and supported a "phased in approach" for Medicare for All.

During that race for the northeastern Ohio seat, Poindexter also expressed his support for law enforcement when he ran campaign ads featuring an Ohio sheriff.

"When you see the world through the prism of outsider, insider—everything makes sense," Green said about the midterm outcomes for Democrats.

"Poindexter ran as an economic populist outsider and spoke to many of those same people who voted for Trump," he added. "I don't think he's run away from his values, but even Trump voters don't self-identify in many cases as being of one ideology. They want someone who's going to shake up a broken economic and political system and stand up to corporate power."

news.title: Why New England’s Republican Governors Withstood the Blue Wave
news.text:
Peter Gallagher, a voter in liberal Townshend, Vt., filled in the ovals for Democrat after Democrat at the polls last Tuesday. But when it came to the race for governor, Mr. Gallagher, 67, made a notable exception: He voted for the Republican incumbent, Gov. Phil Scott.

So did Joanne Davis of Putney, who said she appreciated Mr. Scott’s low-key persona: “He’s a normal person. Not crazy, not scary.”

Vermont voters helped drive the blue wave that stunned the country, casting out two dozen Republicans from the state Legislature and replacing them with Democrats, who regained supermajorities in both chambers. But enough also stuck by Mr. Scott, a soft-spoken moderate, to deliver him a record sixth term, in a state that favored Vice President Kamala Harris over President Trump in 2024 by one of the widest margins in the country.

Mr. Scott’s success in a liberal New England state — and the success of Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican who was re-elected last week in neighboring New Hampshire — offer a glimmer of hope for a party freshly battered by rejection. In different ways, the two governors have survived by leaning into an old-school strain of Republicanism, melding fiscal pragmatism with a moderate approach on social issues. Mr. Scott, in particular, has also explicitly separated himself from President Trump.
news.summary: The low-key approach modeled by Gov. Phil Scott of Vermont and Gov. Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire may gain new relevance as their party looks to recover from a national drubbing.
news.author: Jenna Russell

news.title: Ro Khanna rejects warnings that Trump admin investigations could derail Democrats' affordability agenda
news.text: Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., is brushing off concerns that House Democrats’ eagerness to investigate Trump administration officials could distract the incoming majority from addressing Americans’ concerns about affordability. "I can walk and chew gum at the same time," Khanna told Fox News when asked if the investigations could be a distraction. Democratic lawmakers have repeatedly called to open probes into different allies of President Donald Trump after winning majorities in both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections. BERNIE SANDERS WARNS DEMOCRATS NOT TO SPEND ALL THEIR TIME INVESTIGATING TRUMP Khanna argued that Democrats using their oversight authority to subpoena Trump administration officials and others in his orbit won’t distract from the party’s ability to address affordability issues. "We've got to have accountability, and then we also have to increase the minimum wage," Khanna said. Khanna has been an advocate for impeaching Trump for a third time, saying it would be "setting a standard" of accountability. On NBC’s "Meet the Press," Khanna said that impeaching Trump would show that an administration cannot take action in Iran like he claims Trump has "without constitutional approval." KAMALA HARRIS BREAKS WITH LEFT FLANK, WARNS DEMS THAT IMPEACHING TRUMP IS 'NOT A GOOD IDEA' He told Fox News Digital that conducting investigations to hold Trump and his administration accountable, particularly for the war in Iran, could help lower food and gas prices. "We've gotta end the war in Iran," Khanna said. "That's the biggest thing. We need accountability to end this war, and that would lower food and gas prices."
news.summary: Ro Khanna says Democrats can pursue Trump investigations and tackle affordability at once, arguing accountability for the Iran war would lower prices.

news.title: How Scott Colom defied the odds to go from district attorney to Mississippi's Democratic US Senator
news.text:
JACKSON, Miss. — When Scott Colom, a local district attorney, announced his candidacy late last year, it seemed like a long shot in a ruby red state.

But by October of this year, a month before votes came pouring in for him, he was confident.

"We didn't have hundreds of million dollars to come in to spend – we did it going door to door, festival to festival, earning support," Colom said at a canvassing event on the Mississippi coast. "We're gonna shock a lot of people, but I'm not gonna be shocked. The people of Mississippi are behind this campaign: they understand Mississippi matters."

Colom narrowly defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, according to a race call by The Associated Press on Wednesday evening, marking one of the most stunning upsets of the midterm elections this year.

Flipping red counties with a focus on affordability 

Colom won by less than five thousand votes, with a small fraction of the vote still left to be counted.

While he swept areas of Mississippi that have traditionally leaned left, like Hinds County, home to Jackson, the state capital, he also picked up places that have traditionally voted Republican, like Forrest County, which President Trump won in 2024 with about 58 percent of the vote.

Colom has been the district attorney for the state's 16th judicial district since 2016. That includes his hometown of Columbus, Mississippi, in Lowndes County – an area that's also got a right-leaning voter base.

Colom ran on accessible healthcare, saving rural hospitals and affordability. He said that working in a Republican-majority area informed the need for bipartisanship in tackling those issues.

"I believed that the majority of the Mississippians love our state more than they hate the Democratic party or love the Republican party," Colom said. "They want their kids to have good schools. ... they want to be able to make sure that young people, if they want to stay in Mississippi, can have a job. They want the hospitals to stay open."

While Colom isn't surprised that his message resonated this year with voters, he faced obstacles when a federal judicial nomination stalled in the U.S. Senate in 2023, when then-President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal judgeship.

Mississippi's Sen. Roger Wicker, a Republican, indicated he would support his nomination.

The state's Junior Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith blocked him. She cited donations from billionaire philanthropist George Soros around Colom's run for DA, which in 2023, Colom said were to an independent PAC – not his campaign.

She also said he opposed legislation to protect female athletes in a statement provided to the Mississippi Free Press at the time.

In a letter to Hyde-Smith, Colom said he didn't know what she was referring to and noted that he'd signed a statement saying he wouldn't use law enforcement resources to criminalize doctors who offer gender affirming care to transgender youth.

He also stated in the letter that if he was confirmed as a judge, any of his personal views would be irrelevant to his "daily work." And he asked the senator to reconsider – she didn't.

Three years later, she was defending her seat from him. She was confident, on election night, that she'd beat him, telling her supporters, "I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator."

She instead lost and on Wednesday night, she issued a statement conceding the race, saying she respects the decision of Mississippi voters.

A narrow victory that 'made a difference' 

Colom recognized that attention from national Democratic leaders, and his party's campaign funds, came late this year, but he noted that it was the attention his campaign received from voters within the state that made the difference.

"They understand the power of their vote in ways that we really haven't seen in a long period of time, because if you look at these margins, certainly everything that everybody did made a difference," Colom told reporters in Jackson just days before the election was called.

Being elected as a Democrat is no small feat either. The last time Mississippi sent a Democrat to the Senate was 1982 and an incumbent hasn't been defeated since 1942.

Colom now also holds the distinction of being the state's first Black senator since Reconstruction. 

It's something he's proud of – but not the laurels he's resting on.

"My job is to be a senator that makes it easier for the next African American that has the work ethic, the vision, the values, and they want to be United States senator, make it easier for them," Colom said. "I am a person that is continuing to show up in the community and take the tough questions and explain my, you know, live my values. And if I do that, it makes it easier for the next person to be judged by their character and not their skin color."

While his victory is historic, his campaign has also made waves – especially on social media. In an interview with WLOX, Hyde-Smith responded to questions about beef affordability by suggesting folks pick a different protein.

Colom hit back, with a campaign ad, suggesting folks pick another senator instead.

Eventually, the rest of the country started listening. About two weeks before the election, the PAC associated with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer donated $1.2 million for advertising.

And, several big name Democrats also ended up joining Colom on the campaign trail: former Vice President Kamala Harris, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, former President Bill Clinton and U.S. Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia, to name a few.

Colom traveled the whole state – from the coast to the capital, up to the Tennessee border. While in the Mississippi Delta, he said what he wants to do while in the Senate all goes back to his home of Columbus.

"I've always been committed to trying to make my community better, trying to make my city better, trying to make my state better, and that's what running for United States Senate is all about for me," Colom said. "It's a continuation of a service that runs in my family and I was raised [by] my community and my church to give back and that's why I'm doing it in this moment."

Tiara Jackson of Mississippi Public Broadcasting contributed to this report.
news.summary: In a state that hasn't had a Democrat in office since 1980 and hasn't sent a Black Senator to Washington since the 1870s, Colom's win represents a massive upset in state politics.
news.author: Elise Catrion Gregg

news.title: Trump Taps Campaign Lawyer and Pardon Adviser for Top U.S. Intel Agency
news.text:
As a lawyer on President Donald Trump’s 2024 reelection bid, Gary Lawkowski filed a complaint against the Washington Post for supposedly making an in-kind contribution to the Kamala Harris campaign by buying social media advertising for its articles.

In the White House, he played a pivotal role in the pardons process that rewarded Trump cronies and donors.

Now, Lawkowski could serve in an obscure but crucial role within the nation’s top intelligence agency, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. On Monday, Trump nominated Lawkowski to serve as general counsel of ODNI.

It is unclear when Lawkowski will appear before a confirmation hearing or whether Democrats will look favorably upon him when they take control of the Senate in January. His nomination is already drawing pushback, however, from a progressive group that says it represents another attempt to politicize the ODNI after Trump’s bid to install loyalist Bill Pulte as its director fizzled.

“Lawkowski has been a key player in Trump’s corrupt pardon scheme and his nomination tells us that the administration is trying to stack the intelligence community with cronies so they can further weaponize it against their perceived political opponents and innocent Americans,” Hajar Hammado, senior policy adviser at Demand Progress, said in a statement. “Senators must oppose his nomination.”

The ODNI is a relatively small agency, and it doesn’t hoover up its own raw data. As the only intelligence body operating at the Cabinet level, however, it is tasked with coordinating and overseeing intelligence collection and analysis at other spy agencies like the CIA and National Security Agency.

Under former Director Tulsi Gabbard, the ODNI took an unusually prominent role in declassifying information that cast a negative light on Trump’s enemies or fed into right-wing obsessions, such as the Covid lab-leak controversy.

The general counsel plays an important role in interpreting spying law — meaning that Lawkowski could either facilitate or block intelligence community abuses.

In recent months, Trump has displayed an unusual interest in the ODNI, installing housing czar Pulte to replace Gabbard before bipartisan pushback forced him to tap former prosecutor Jay Clayton as a permanent replacement.

In his current role at the White House, Lawkowski serves as deputy assistant and deputy counsel to the president, according to his most recent ethics disclosure, and it is unclear whether he has relevant national security experience.

There is ample evidence that he is a loyalist to Trump. As a lawyer on the Trump campaign, he blasted off a complaint to the Federal Election Commission claiming that the Washington Post’s online advertisements about stories on Trump represented an in-kind contribution to Harris’s campaign. Campaign finance law experts said the claim was baseless. Lawkowski also represented Trump in litigation over the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.

In the White House, he has helped decide who does and does not receive pardons, according to reporting last year in the New York Times. Under Trump, the White House has asserted authority over a pardons process that traditionally flowed through the Department of Justice.

Trump’s blanket clemency for January 6, 2021, insurrectionists preceded a parade of pardons for people who donated to his campaign or causes, or Republican officials who had been convicted of corruption, drawing widespread criticism.

One of the many who received a Trump pardon was former Tennessee state senator Brian Kelsey, who had been represented by Lawkowski before the lawyer went to the White House. Lawkowski did not respond to a request for comment on whether he recused himself from that pardon.

It is unclear whether Senate Select Committee on Intelligence Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark., will push to have Lawkowski confirmed before the next Senate is sworn in on January 3. The Senate is dealing with a cramped calendar before the end of the year. (Cotton’s office declined to comment.)

The likely incoming intelligence chair, Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., was harshly critical of Trump’s temporary appointment of Pulte at the ODNI. He ultimately voted against Clayton’s nomination after touting him as a more acceptable alternative to Pulte. (Warner’s office did not respond to a request for comment.)

Lawkowski was tapped to replace John “Jack” Dever, who was confirmed by the Senate to serve as general counsel a little over a year ago. Dever joined the government-backed mortgage finance company Freddie Mac as its executive counsel and vice president in September, according to its website. (Dever left the ODNI with Director Jay Clayton’s blessing and remains well-respected at the agency, an ODNI spokesperson said.)

Dever’s resume included extensive work in the national security realm as a Korean linguist for the U.S. Army, an assistance general counsel at the FBI, and a counter-terror prosecutor in Illinois.
