news.title: Kim Kardashian's MAGA ties and SKIMS Israel expansion are under fire after Lewis Hamilton's Gaza visit: 'He’s going out with a raging Zionist'
news.text: Kim Kardashian is facing fresh criticism over her political connections and business interests after Lewis Hamilton's visit to the Rafah border crossing brought their relationship into the spotlight. The seven-time Formula 1 world champion travelled to Egypt on November 10 to witness humanitarian aid operations for Gaza. A day later, he called Israel's actions in the territory genocide and demanded that aid trucks be allowed through.His comments have prompted social media users to revisit Kardashian's SKIMS expansion into Israel, a reported event involving families of Israeli soldiers and her longstanding connections to Donald Trump's family. The contrast has triggered questions about the couple's public positions.Hamilton's visit to Egypt's Rafah border crossing on November 10, 2026, was intended to give him a closer look at humanitarian operations for Gaza. The Ferrari driver toured Egyptian Red Crescent warehouses in El-Arish, where he met aid workers and received briefings about the preparation and transportation of relief supplies. He also saw trucks carrying essential supplies waiting to enter Gaza. According to Hamilton, some deliveries faced lengthy delays or were rejected, including sleeping bags, first-aid kits, medical equipment, wheelchairs and footballs intended for children.In an Instagram post on November 11, Hamilton wrote: "The past three years of Israel's genocide in Gaza is appalling." He described the situation as an injustice and said no human being should be treated as though their life matters less. He also described Gaza as feeling like an "open-air prison" before making a direct demand: "Israel needs to fulfil its obligations under the ceasefire and let the aid trucks in. No excuse."Hamilton's statement received widespread attention, but it also brought his relationship with Kardashian into the discussion. Critics began questioning how his public advocacy for Palestinians fits alongside his girlfriend's business interests and associations. Israel strongly denies accusations of genocide.One of the biggest points of criticism concerns SKIMS, Kardashian's shapewear and clothing company. The brand officially entered the Israeli market in November 2025 through an exclusive partnership with Irani Corp, the retail group behind Factory 54. SKIMS began online sales through Factory 54 on November 10, followed by dedicated shopping spaces inside selected outlets. Plans for standalone stores were also announced, with the first locations including Ramat Aviv Mall and Big Fashion Glilot.The expansion became controversial among people supporting boycotts of businesses operating in Israel amid the Gaza conflict. For critics, the decision raised questions about the commercial presence of a celebrity-owned brand in a country facing international scrutiny over its military campaign. Another issue concerns a reported private shopping event organised by SKIMS for daughters and families of Israeli soldiers in Los Angeles in late 2025. The event was reportedly connected to Hagiborim, an organisation supporting children of fallen or injured IDF personnel.A deleted Instagram Story from the organisation thanking Kardashian and her friend Allison Statter reportedly resurfaced online. Critics questioned why the brand was associated with an event involving military families while humanitarian conditions in Gaza remained dire. The reported event has added another dimension to the criticism. However, it is important to distinguish the documented SKIMS retail partnership from the less independently established details surrounding the private shopping event.Kim Kardashian's political associations have also become a major part of the discussion. Although she has never formally endorsed Donald Trump or declared herself a MAGA supporter, her longstanding friendship with his daughter Ivanka Trump has repeatedly attracted attention. The two have known each other for years and were first photographed together at the 2014 Met Gala. Their friendship became particularly visible in November 2024, when Kardashian shared several photographs with Ivanka to celebrate her birthday. "No one sweeter than you @ivankatrump," she wrote, adding three heart emojis.The timing attracted criticism, as the birthday tribute came just days before the US presidential election. Kardashian had not publicly endorsed a candidate in the 2024 race, but some users interpreted the affectionate post as a sign of her political leanings. Things became more controversial on January 20, 2025, when Kardashian shared a photograph of Melania Trump arriving at Donald Trump's second presidential inauguration. The SKIMS founder posted the image on her Instagram Story without a caption or explanation.The post quickly attracted reactions on X. One user wrote: "Kim kardashian posted a photo of melania trump? Yeah its clear who she voted for." Another commented: "idk why i still followed kim kardashian honestly but her posting a pic of melania at the inauguration on her story was like immediate unfollow bye you out of touch psychopath." Another user wrote: "Successful billionaire, Kim Kardashian, has posted Melanie Trump on her Instagram story. We know who she voted for." Kardashian's connection to Melania is not established as a personal friendship. Rather, it was her decision to share the First Lady's photograph that prompted questions about whether she was signalling support for the returning Trump administration.Her association with Elon Musk has also contributed to the discussion. Kardashian has previously shared content featuring Tesla's Optimus robot, while Musk has been a prominent supporter of Trump. Critics have brought up these interactions alongside her friendships with the Trump family. However, Kardashian's political history is not exclusively Republican. She supported Hillary Clinton in the 2016 presidential election and worked with the Trump administration on criminal justice reform, particularly the campaign for Alice Marie Johnson's release from prison. She also celebrated Joe Biden and Kamala Harris's victory in 2020. Therefore, describing Kardashian as a confirmed MAGA supporter would be inaccurate. Her political associations have been mixed, even as her friendships and social media activity continue to attract scrutiny.The backlash has largely centred on whether Hamilton and Kardashian can maintain a relationship despite what critics perceive as contrasting public positions on Israel and Palestine. A Reddit user captured the central question in a social media post: "Can two people be in a relationship when they have such different world views?"The post specifically highlighted Hamilton's visit to organisations supporting Gaza aid while Kardashian's brand continues to operate in Israel. Some users have also questioned whether Hamilton's public statements lose credibility when his partner has commercial interests in the country. Others have pointed to the reported shopping event involving IDF families as another reason for criticism.The Melania Trump post has also resurfaced in these discussions, with users revisiting Kardashian's previous associations with the Trump family. One recurring criticism is that her public relationships and business decisions deserve the same scrutiny as her statements and social media activity. However, not everyone agrees that Hamilton should be held responsible for Kardashian's business decisions. Some users have argued that two people can maintain a relationship without sharing identical political opinions. Others believe that a person's professional associations should not automatically determine their partner's beliefs. The discussion has also raised questions about celebrity activism, particularly whether public figures should be judged by their own statements or by the people and companies they associate with.
news.author: Nillohit Bagchi

news.title: Joe Biden Reveals What’s So ‘Disturbing’ About Donald Trump’s White House Makeover
news.text:
Former President Joe Biden pulled no punches when People magazine asked for his reaction to predecessor-turned-successor Donald Trump’s demolition of the White House’s East Wing to make way for his controversial ballroom.

“Almost as disturbing as the gold bars on the walls of the White House and the Oval Office,” Biden replied in a new interview ahead of the release of his forthcoming memoir, “Promise Me, America.”

Read the interview at People.

“I mean, what the hell are we talking about? I find it disturbing,” Biden continued. “I’ve viewed the president’s judgment in tearing down the East Wing and a number of other things as nothing more than to try to create monuments to himself: ‘I built that.’ I find it beneath the country.”

Biden also opened up about his diagnosis with an aggressive form of prostate cancer that has spread to his bones, saying he wouldn’t have sought reelection in 2024 had he known the disease was why he was “feeling lousy.”

“I don’t think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running for [president],” he said.

“But that wasn’t the case,” he added, noting that he believed he had “the capacity” and was “the best-equipped person” for the role.

Biden later abandoned his campaign and endorsed his vice president, Kamala Harris, who subsequently lost to Trump.

Watch part of the interview on YouTube. 

The former president also weighed in on Republicans’ drubbing in last week’s midterm elections, saying he didn’t think the results “could have gone any better.”

“I was very happy,” he said. “I was worried whether they [the American people] were going to fall for just the bravado of the Republican leadership and Trump in particular, but they weren’t.”
news.author: Lee Moran

news.title: The midterm earthquake in Texas could redraw America’s electoral map
news.text:
The midterms are done and dusted. The resounding defeat American voters delivered to President Donald Trump and the Republican Party is one for the ages. It carries lessons that future occupants of the White House would do well to remember.
Amid the Democratic victories across the country, one state stands out: Texas.
For more than three decades, the Lone Star State has been a seemingly impregnable Republican fortress. On November 3, that fortress came crashing down.
Democrat James Talarico defeated scandal-plagued Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, Trump’s preferred candidate, in the US Senate race, winning approximately 55 per cent of the vote against Paxton’s 43 per cent. Nearly 1.2 million votes separated the candidates.
Talarico, a member of the Texas House of Representatives since 2018, accomplished what generations of Democrats had struggled to achieve: winning a US Senate seat in Texas. The party had not won one since 1988.
The gubernatorial result was equally remarkable.
Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, ending 32 years of Republican control of the governor’s mansion.
Hinojosa, a state representative of Mexican heritage, secured approximately 53% of the vote against Abbott’s 46%, becoming the first Democrat elected Texas governor since Ann Richards in 1990.
The Democratic breakthrough extended far beyond these two marquee contests.
The party captured the Texas House of Representatives, the lieutenant governorship and the attorney general’s office. Democrats also won important judicial contests, breaking another longstanding pattern of Republican dominance in statewide elections.
For a party that had spent decades struggling to win statewide office, November 3 was nothing short of extraordinary.
The importance of Texas to Republican politics cannot be overstated.
It is America’s second-most-populous state and has the nation’s second-largest economy, trailing only California on both counts.
Texas is also the largest state in the contiguous United States, with a land mass greater than that of South India.
But its potential political importance lies in the Electoral College. Texas has 40 electoral votes, making it the country’s second-largest presidential prize after California.
For decades, Republicans have built their presidential strategies around the assumption that Texas would remain firmly in their column. Democrats, meanwhile, have enjoyed a similarly reliable advantage in California and New York, which together account for 82 electoral votes.
Texas, along with Florida’s 30 electoral votes, has been central to the Republican counterweight. The 2026 results have suddenly thrown that calculation into question.
Imagine a Democratic presidential nominee beginning the electoral contest with California, New York and Texas effectively secured. That would mean 122 electoral votes from just three states — nearly halfway to the 270 required to win the presidency.
For Republicans, losing Texas in a presidential election would make an already complicated electoral map significantly more difficult.
Perhaps the most striking feature of the Texas results is the sheer number of votes Democrats received. Talarico won approximately 5.45 million votes, while Hinojosa received more than 5.23 million.
Compare those figures with the 2024 presidential election. Donald Trump carried Texas with nearly 6.4 million votes, defeating Kamala Harris, who received approximately 4.84 million. Both Democratic candidates in 2026 received substantially more votes than their party’s presidential nominee had attracted just two years earlier.
Their Republican opponents, meanwhile, fell dramatically short of Trump’s 2024 total. Paxton received approximately 4.25 million votes, while Abbott secured about 4.52 million.
This is especially significant because presidential elections traditionally attract substantially higher turnout than midterms.
The numbers suggest that Democrats succeeded in mobilising their voters while also attracting some independents and Republicans disillusioned with the direction of their party. Trump’s handling of the Iran war, rising petrol prices, persistent affordability concerns, tariffs and aggressive immigration enforcement all contributed to the political environment.
Paxton’s personal controversies added another dimension to the Senate contest. But the Republican defeat cannot be attributed solely to voters changing sides. Turnout also mattered.
Many voters who supported Trump in 2024 did not return to the polls in 2026, while others appear to have crossed party lines. The result was a remarkable reversal in a state Trump had carried by nearly 14 percentage points just two years earlier.
Could Texas become another California? For Democrats, the result opens an extraordinary opportunity to redraw America’s political map. Turning Texas blue has been a long-term ambition. Now, for the first time in decades, it appears more achievable.
There are historical parallels worth considering. California, the home state of Republican presidents Richard Nixon and Ronald Reagan, was once competitive territory for both major parties. But the Republican Party’s embrace of restrictive immigration policies under Governor Pete Wilson in the 1990s helped alienate Latino voters and contributed to the state’s transformation into a Democratic stronghold.
Texas shares some important demographic characteristics with California. Both are majority-minority states with large Hispanic populations, accounting for roughly two-fifths of their residents.
Demographics alone, however, do not determine political outcomes. Texas has its own political traditions, economic structure and electorate that will affect the results.
The question is whether the Democrats can turn their 2026 breakthrough into a durable political realignment.
There is absolutely no guarantee that Texas will remain blue. History offers a reminder of how quickly political fortunes can change.
In 1994, George W. Bush defeated Democratic Governor Ann Richards, beginning an era of Republican dominance. Working with his chief political strategist, Karl Rove, Bush helped build an organisational machine that transformed Texas politics.
Before that Republican resurgence, Democrats had controlled the governor’s mansion for most of the preceding century, interrupted only by Republican Bill Clements’ two non-consecutive terms.
Bush’s victory was not merely an isolated electoral success. It marked the beginning of a political transformation that lasted more than three decades.
Democrats now have an opportunity to attempt something similar.
But winning one election — even an extraordinary one — is not the same as building a lasting majority. The party must demonstrate that it can govern effectively, retain its newly assembled coalition and persuade voters that its victories were more than a temporary reaction against Trump.
Republicans, for their part, must confront the reasons so many Texans abandoned or stayed away from their candidates. The 2028 presidential election will provide a crucial test.
If Democrats can replicate their 2026 performance, the consequences for Republican presidential ambitions could be enormous.
For now, one thing is certain: Texas can no longer be taken for granted. And that may prove to be the most consequential political lesson of the 2026 midterms.
(Frank F. Islam, an entrepreneur, philanthropist and civic leader based in the Washington, DC, area, is a Democratic Party donor and fundraiser. The views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost's views.)

news.title: Donald Trump's Secret Letter to Joe Biden Finally Revealed, Showing Astonishing Message Left in Oval Office
news.text: US President Donald Trump left Joe Biden a surprisingly warm handwritten letter when he departed the White House in January 2021, despite spending months attacking his election rival and refusing to accept his defeat.The message, written in Trump's trademark black Sharpie, has now been revealed in Biden's forthcoming memoir, offering an unexpected glimpse into the private relationship between two presidents whose public exchanges were frequently hostile.Trump praised Biden's love for America, urged him to make his mark on history and wished him well as he prepared to take over the Oval Office.What Trump Wrote in His Secret Letter to BidenThe two-page letter was written on official White House stationery and dated 20 January 2021, the day Biden was inaugurated as America's 46th president. It was placed in an envelope addressed 'To 46' and began with the greeting 'Dear Joe.'According to the photocopy reviewed by The New York Times and the account in Biden's book, Trump opened by describing working in the Oval Office as a 'blessing beyond imagination.'He encouraged his successor to remember the presidents who had occupied the office before him and consider the legacy he wanted to leave behind.'You now have the opportunity to choose your place in history, and I know you will be true to yourself and the American people,' Trump wrote.He also suggested that previous presidents had largely been swept along by history rather than changing its course, adding that he believed Biden would be different because of his love for the American people.Trump ended the message by wishing Biden and his wife, Jill, well, writing, 'May God bless you and Jill, and may God bless America!'Biden Surprised by Unexpectedly Warm MessageBiden had previously acknowledged receiving a letter from Trump on his first day in office but declined to disclose its contents, describing it as private and 'very generous.'In his forthcoming memoir, 'Promise Me, America,' Biden explains that the message surprised him because of the hostility that had characterised their political relationship. He described the contrast as feeling like there were 'two Donald Trumps,' with the private letter offering best wishes in language that sounded as though it came from an old friend.The gesture was particularly notable because Trump had challenged the results of the 2020 presidential election and declined to attend Biden's inauguration.Trump Told Biden They Could Have Been Good FriendsThe letter was not the only unexpectedly friendly exchange Biden recalled in his memoir. The former president also described a meeting with Trump at the White House on 13 November 2024, shortly after the Republican defeated Kamala Harris in the presidential election.According to Biden, Trump adopted a remarkably friendly tone during their conversation, leaving him wondering whether the president-elect was putting him on.Trump reportedly told him: 'You know, Joe, if it weren't for politics, I believe we'd be good friends.'He then suggested that the pair might have spent their time golfing together if politics had not come between them. Biden wrote that he was too stunned to respond immediately and did not understand why Trump was being so complimentary. He eventually redirected the conversation towards the business at hand.
news.author: Michael Toledo

news.title: Scott Colom Wins Historic Mississippi Senate Race After Eight-Day Count - The Daily Scrum News
news.text:
JACKSON, Miss. — Eight days after the polls officially closed, the grueling U.S. Senate race in Mississippi reached its historical conclusion as Democratic candidate Scott Colom unseated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. The Associated Press called the election after a long, meticulous count of affidavit and absentee ballots that saw Colom build an unassailable lead of roughly 2,500 votes, finishing with 49.1% to Hyde-Smith’s 48.8%. The victory marks a monumental shift in Southern politics, delivering the state its first Democratic U.S. senator in 44 years and its first Black U.S. senator since the Reconstruction era ended over a century ago.

Colom, a district attorney from Columbus, Mississippi, becomes only the third Black senator to represent the state in Washington. The previous two, Hiram Revels and Blanche K. Bruce, were elected by the state legislature during Reconstruction in the 1870s. Not since 1874 has a Black candidate won a U.S. Senate seat in Mississippi, making Colom the first Black senator elected by popular vote in the state’s history. Furthermore, no Democrat had captured a Senate seat in Mississippi since John C. Stennis won reelection in 1982. Colom’s win shatters a decades-long Republican stronghold and signals a dramatic realignment in a state long considered politically immovable.

The campaign unfolded against a broader national backdrop of Democratic momentum, but Colom’s victory was built primarily on an aggressive, unconventional local strategy. Leveraging Mississippi’s demographic makeup, the state has the highest percentage of Black residents in the nation, Colom focused heavily on grassroots turnout while simultaneously pitching a moderate policy platform aimed at rural working-class voters. He campaigned on economic relief, maternal healthcare improvements, border security, and Second Amendment rights, directly engaging voters in traditionally conservative strongholds. Colom routinely met voters in person across all eighty-two counties, even handing out free food from a mobile taco truck to foster open conversations in skeptical communities.

In contrast, political analysts noted that Hyde-Smith ran a low-profile campaign, largely relying on traditional party loyalty and high-profile endorsements. While national figures like former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris aided Colom in the final stretch, the Democratic nominee carried much of the early load himself, running a lean campaign that gained national attention only as polling narrowed in the closing weeks. When the initial election night numbers left the candidates deadlocked, law teams from both parties descended on Jackson to monitor the tabulation of outstanding ballots. The count steadily favored Colom as urban centers and high-turnout rural precincts reported their remaining tallies.

Upon the race being called, Hyde-Smith conceded, wishing Colom well as he prepares to assume office. National party leaders celebrated the win as a major breakthrough for Southern Democrats, while civil rights organizations hailed the outcome as a testament to persistent voter turnout in the deep South. Colom’s historic victory not only changes the structural balance of power in the U.S. Senate but also redefines the boundaries of political competitiveness across the region.
news.author: Kingston Bailey

news.title: Scott Colom Wins Mississippi, Becomes State's 1st Black Senator Since 1874
news.text: Democratic nominee Scott Colom defeated Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday in Mississippi's closely contested US Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black US senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.Colom's narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations despite having the largest share of Black residents of any US state. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the American South.The Associated Press called the contest Wednesday in Colom's favor after local elections officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi."While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," Hyde-Smith, 67, said in a two-minute concession speech posted online. "I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state."A spokesman for the senator said she called Colom to congratulate him and concede before the video was shared publicly.READ | Saba Haider Credits Ghaziabad Upbringing For Her Public Life, US WinColom scheduled a victory celebration with supporters Wednesday night in Jackson.The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith's missteps as she sought a second full term."They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they're going through," Colom said in the campaign's closing stretch.Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society."It's got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America - a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better," he said.Party leaders hailed the senator-elect's triumph, with nods to the South's emerging battleground status after other upset victories from North Carolina to Texas."Scott Colom is the only person who could've gotten this done," Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York posted online. "Along with his staff and volunteers, Scott ran the campaign of a lifetime and re-imagined what's possible for Democrats in the South."Former President Bill Clinton, a native Arkansan who campaigned with Colom days before the election, addressed the senator-elect on social media, saying he won "because you believe in the promise of your state's people. And they believed in you right back."Vera Finley was among those supporters, and she arrived early Wednesday to Colom's victory party."I am here to celebrate my parents and my grandparents. I am not one generation out of the cotton fields," Finley said. "Both of my parents picked cotton. And my great grandmother was sold here as a slave from Virginia to here. So I am so excited to be on this side of history."Another Mississippian, NAACP President Derrick Johnson, issued a statement saying the state's voters "made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out.""In a state that has witnessed some of the nation's most difficult battles for voting rights, Black voters once again demonstrated the power of civic engagement and the strength of our democracy," Johnson said.Despite Schumer's support, the contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, finally drawing attention and money months after Black senators, including Georgia's Raphael Warnock and Maryland's Angela Alsobrooks, first urged donors and party leaders to see Mississippi as winnable.The son of a onetime Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Colom garnered attention for his aggressive campaign as Democrats widened the Senate battleground map and Hyde-Smith's vulnerabilities crystallized.He produced of the year's most widely circulated ads. After Hyde-Smith seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they'd "pick another senator instead."When Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, in late October for a rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited outside the gates. He introduced himself, asked about their concerns and explained his priorities.Later that evening, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said nine words in six seconds: "Is this not the best president in our lifetime?"Then she stepped away.Colom's appearance outside the rally tracked his strategy of criticizing Trump's policies - especially the Iran war and tariffs that he said were especially hard on Mississippi farmers - without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a nonentity in Washington - a critique that resonated in a state accustomed to long-serving senators like Thad Cochran, Trent Lott and John Stennis, who all rose to powerful posts and routed federal money back to Mississippi.There is some irony to Hyde-Smith losing to Colom. In 2022, then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a US District Court judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Mississippi's senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Governor Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination.Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom's confirmation under the Senate tradition that members can spike a president's choices for federal judicial positions in their home state. Colom said his campaign was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith.The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist and died in front of his family."In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection," Colom said, telling the story of Evers' military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction."He was killed for helping Mississippians vote," Colom said. "On Tuesday, use your vote and honour everyone who died for that right."Schumer helped Colom raise money, and he drew financial support from other outside players, including Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a billionaire and potential presidential candidate.Former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned on Colom's behalf in the campaign's closing weeks.Because of the Black population and its alignment with Democrats, Mississippi's general elections have been closer for years than its immediate Southern neighbours. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Governor Tate Reeves managed to win reelection by a margin of just 3 percentage points.Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican voter discontent and an uptick in Democrats' usual share of the white vote in Mississippi.Results showed strong turnout in the Mississippi Delta and its concentration of majority Black counties. But nearly all of the state moved leftward from the 2024 election, when Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points.Then-Governor Phil Bryant first appointed Hyde-Smith, who was state agriculture commissioner, to the Senate in 2018 when Cochran resigned. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former US agriculture secretary who'd also been Mississippi's first Black congressman since Reconstruction.During the extended vote count, Colom acknowledged the historic nature of doing what Espy could not. But he said he sees his place more in terms of other Mississippians, especially its youngest residents, than his individual story."My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young Black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision, and the values," he said, "and they want to be United States senator, that nobody says because of anything I've done that they shouldn't get a chance."(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: Because of the Black population and its alignment with Democrats, Mississippi's general elections have been closer for years than its immediate Southern neighbours.
news.author: Associated Press

news.title: How spectacular Republican own goals helped Mississippi make history
news.text:
Democrat Scott Colom was humble in claiming victory late Wednesday night, seizing an eighth Senate seat from the Republicans, this one in the heart of the red south.

“All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” he said. “In the Mississippi, our prayers have often changed the course of history.”

Colom had not just changed history, he had defied it.

Mississippi has a 36 per cent Black population, more than any other state. But the last time it had a Democratic senator, he was an ardent segregationist first elected in 1947 who Atlantic magazine once described as “one of twentieth century America’s most admired white supremacists”.

The last time Mississippi had a Black senator, he was the son of a slave mother and a white planter, born 20 years before the start of the American Civil War. That man, Republican Blanche Bruce, spoke in the Senate against the “flagrant wrongs” that persisted in Mississippi, where Democrats co-ordinated efforts to suppress the Black vote.

More than 150 years later, the names of the parties have changed. But some of the tactics look familiar. Colom’s win represents a spectacular own goal for Republicans, who have long used controversial tactics to keep the state in their – white -hands. This time, they overreached.

‘All I did was have the courage’

Associated Press called the result for Colom, a 43 year-old former prosecutor and judge, on Wednesday night, more than a week after the election. AP put him ahead by 4669 votes, or 0.5 per cent of the 962,237 counted. 

Jubliant supporters gathered in Jackson, Mississippi, one of the most high-profile battlegrounds of the civil rights movement, where Black activists fought – and some died – for democracy.

The victory rally was held on the lawn outside Woodworth Chapel, a meeting ground for prominent civil rights leaders in the 1960s and 1970s, including Martin Luther King, Jr.

“There were many times where I had to have faith,” Colom told supporters. “There were times that I couldn’t get donors to answer the phone. They did not believe a moment like this was possible. But I kept the faith.

“There were times when I did my first town hall in Jackson, Mississippi… Less than ten people showed up. But I kept the faith.”

All year, Colom has insisted he could win the seat.

“But every time I said it, I pointed out that people were going to give me too much credit for it,” he said. “Because it’s not something that I did, y’all. It’s something that we did.

“All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this.”

There is no recount law in Mississippi. The defeated Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, conceded on social media on Wednesday saying: “While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters.”

In a twist of fate, the Republican beaten by Colom could have given him a different career.

In 2022, Colom was nominated by President Joe Biden to be a district court judge.

But Hyde-Smith used her Senate powers to personally prevent the appointment. On election night, when she thought she had won, she even boasted to supporters: “I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge and you blocked him from being a U.S senator.”

Hyde-Smith said her team had worked to ensure every legal vote was counted, and it was a “fair and transparent” election.

‘Barriers for voters of colour’ 

In the era of overt racial segregation in America’s south, the “colour line” was used to refer to the physical and bureaucratic barriers that stood in the way of Black people.

Officials would use tactics like hiding voter registration books from Black would-be voters, and hold white-only primaries.

Modern tactics are marginally less overt.

A Jim Crow era provision still imposes a lifetime voting ban for certain felony convictions, affecting nearly 70,000 people. In August, the Campaign Legal Center said a Republican-led mass closure of polling places particularly disadvantaged voters of colour and low-income voters. It followed a 2013 Supreme Court decision gutting protections against discriminatory voting laws.

“Many Southern localities have taken full advantage of this freedom from federal oversight to impose hard-to-spot practices that create barriers for voters of color in every election,” the CLC found.

Then, in April, the Supreme Court made a decision some dubbed “the worst ruling in a century” and “judicial vandalism“.

In Louisiana v Callais, the six Republican-appointed justices removed what was left of federal protections for minority voters, giving a green light to states to gerrymander districts on racial grounds. Across the country, encouraged by Donald Trump, Republican-majority states started redrawing maps to dilute the Black Democrat vote. Mississippi’s governor declared he would call the state legislature back for a special session to apply a new, openly racial gerrymander.

On top of all this, shortly before the election, more than 230,000 voters were designated inactive. It was the result of a mishandled attempt to “clean the rolls”, initiated by a Republican official. And it disproportionately affected young voters, more likely to vote Democrat.

But the efforts may have backfired. 

Professor D’Andra Orey of Jackson State University told the Pulitzer Center that the rolls issue, and the redistricting attempts, inspired a surge in Black voter turnout.

“Some people actually really literally thought that they were going to lose their right to vote, which then mobilised them to get out the vote,” he said.

It was not the only issue, but it was a big one, he said.

Derrick Johnson, president of Black voting rights organisation NAACP, said: “In a state that has witnessed some of the nation’s most difficult battles for voting rights, Black voters once again demonstrated the power of civic engagement and the strength of our democracy.

“The Trump Administration tried every trick in the book to block voters from the polls, but we showed up and showed out, and we voted.”

‘Blue Mississippi’

Hyde-Smith also helped Colom with unforced errors during her campaign – at one point telling consumers worried about the price of beef to “pick another protein”.

But campaign insiders put Colom’s victory mainly down to his relentless campaigning, which put him in a position to pick up high-profile Democrat support and fundraising late in the day, once the seat looked winnable.

This week Colom complained that, for most of the campaign cycle, analysts had assessed his seat as solid Republican, which “made it much more difficult to fundraise and [is] part of the reason the South has been neglected for so long”.

news.title: Trump's Veterans Day Message Compared to Those of Potential 2028 Contenders
news.text: President Donald Trump used his Veterans Day address at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday to honor U.S. service members while highlighting his administration's military record, veterans policies and foreign policy priorities. Trump praised the sacrifices of those who served in uniform and said Americans owed an enduring debt to veterans. "On Veterans Day, we honor those who have worn the uniform, who have worn the battle, who have stood to watch, whose ranks have formed the mighty wall of flesh and blood, of bravery and devotion that has defended our freedom for 250 years," Trump said. He pointed to record military recruiting numbers, improvements in veterans' care and America's renewed strength on the world stage as accomplishments of his administration. "Our republic has triumphed, and today our country is stronger than it has ever been before," Trump said. The president referenced U.S. operations involving Iran and Venezuela, argued that American military power had been restored under his leadership and contrasted his administration's handling of veterans' issues with that of previous administrations. He also touted his most recent construction project. “Soon, we’re going to dedicate a magnificent triumphal arch to our veterans,” Trump told the crowd at Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Virginia. “And that’s in honor of our great veterans and our great military. They’ve been waiting for it for 200 years." Potential 2028 Republican Contenders Although the 2028 Republican presidential race has yet to take shape, Vice President JD Vance has consistently been viewed as an early front-runner in polling and prediction markets. Other Republicans frequently mentioned as potential contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis. This is not a comprehensive list. JD Vance Vance, who served in the U.S. Marine Corps from 2003 to 2007, recognized three World War II veterans alongside Trump at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday. “One of the most important things our veterans do is not just fight for their country; they fight for their fellow veterans," Vance told the crowd. "And let me say, as one veteran to the next, we are picking up that torch every single day. We will never leave our veterans behind.” Marco Rubio Rubio, who is in Paris for the G7 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, released a video message on One America News Network, urging Americans to care for military members and their families. news.title: America’s Economy Is Becoming Two-Tiered
news.text:
Cornell University is in the news and for all the wrong reasons. Yet whatever you think of the horrendous frat scandal that’s been dominating social media conversation, there’s one angle to the story, and to Cornell more generally, that’s gone largely unexplored: class. 

Recent research backs up what we already know: the wealthy have a much easier time getting into elite schools like Cornell than everyone else. That elite education then places these young adults at even greater advantage, with Ivy League graduates wildly overrepresented among Fortune 500 CEOs, the New York Times editorial board, and other top institutions.

America’s education system, in other words, is two-tiered, with elite liberal schools producing elite liberal graduates who go on to staff elite liberal institutions. High-achieving students from the State University at Buffalo, where I went to college, are overlooked in favor of unremarkable graduates of a deeply troubled school like Cornell 150 miles away.

This trend is becoming endemic. America is becoming a two-tiered country, where liberal politics overlay across economic elitism, where the privileged class gets ahead and even get special treatment while everyone else struggles to get by. 

Many conservatives have been warning about this divergence for years. Now, the data increasingly backs them up.

Last year, a term began to circulate among researchers studying inflation: K-shaped economy. The idea is that the wealthy are getting wealthier thanks to a rising stock market, growing corporate earnings, and executive payouts, while the middle and working classes are left to contend with sharp inflation, stagnant wages, and an unaffordable housing market.

In other words, America’s economy is becoming two-tiered. While most of the economic indicators look good, many of the gains are felt by that largely leftist upper demographic.

The left loves to decry income inequality, but they leave out that they’re the ones benefiting from it. The wealthiest ZIP codes in America overwhelmingly vote Democrat and are concentrated in blue states like New York, California, and Connecticut. In 2024, the highest income bracket in the United States voted for Kamala Harris while the lowest voted for Donald Trump.

With this economic and political tiering comes cultural tiering, as Whole Foods shoppers, cyclists, Saturday Night Live viewers, and elite newspapers readers all tend to have higher incomes than the average American. You might even say performatively worrying about income inequality you benefit from is a hallmark of upper-tier America.

What’s worse is that these tiers are becoming institutionalized across the American economy. Corporations are increasingly crafting profit models around that upper tier, a divide that’s reflected in their business practices.

From Disney World’s “Lightning Lanes” to ski slopes to airports, expedited service for the wealthy is becoming a baked-in feature. CNN notes that dating app Tinder has even gotten in on the game, advertising a “skip the line” feature that prioritizes a user’s profile for a cool $500 a month.

These trends are culturally troubling, of course, but also nothing new in a market economy. An even bigger problem — one that happens to be a public policy concern as it’s banned under antitrust laws — arises when dominant companies use their market power to enforce tiers, shutting out competitors, restricting consumer choice, and undermining competition.

Perhaps the most disturbing example of this kind of two-tiered service is in the real estate sector. Home sales have long centered on Multiple Listing Services (MLS), shared databases where real estate agents post homes for sale so other agents can find them for their clients. Those listings are then displayed on public websites like Zillow and Redfin, allowing everyday Americans to see what’s available.

Not in two-tiered America. The real estate brokerage Compass (the nation’s largest) has begun withholding some listings from public websites, instead giving select buyers an early look through private networks. It has even gone so far as to financially incentivize some agents to remove their listings from the public’s view. 

 The result? At a time when Americans are already struggling to afford a place to live, some may not even get to see which homes are for sale unless they have access to the right brokerage or its private network. Unsurprisingly, this has led to an investigation from the GOP-led House Judiciary antitrust subcommittee and high-profile consumer protection lawsuits.

All this is moving in a predictable political direction. A recent Fox News poll found that 65 percent of Americans think the economy is rigged to favor the wealthy. Meanwhile, Generation Z is more favorable toward socialism than capitalism while 39 percent nationally express that view.

These young socialists ignore not only that those getting ahead in two-tiered America are likely to agree with them, but that socialism would only make the tiering much worse. A socialist state far more than a capitalist one empowers and enriches its ruling class at the expense of everyone else.

What we need is to fix the America we have. We need policymakers willing to stand up and challenge two-tiered America. These reforms should naturally come from the political right, which has turned populist under Donald Trump and been vindicated on many of these trends.

A left that benefits from inequality is a left that will never act against inequality. It’s time to restore the American dream and make sure the rest of us can get a fair shake.

Michael Caputo is a longtime political advisor and communications specialist who served as assistant secretary of public affairs in the Department of Health and Human Services in the first Trump administration

news.title: 'Blue Mississippi sure has a nice ring to it': Democrats react to Colom's win
news.text:
Democratic challenger Scott Colom's upset victory over Republican incumbent Hyde-Smith immediately drew reaction from prominent Democratic leaders across the country, who framed the result as both an historic breakthrough in Mississippi and one of the most significant victories of the 2026 midterm elections.

Colom's victory capped a campaign that transformed what was once considered a long-shot Democratic bid into one of the nation's most closely watched Senate contests.

A longtime district attorney, Scott Colom built his campaign around economic issues, government accountability and expanding opportunities in rural communities while drawing support from national Democratic figures, including former President Bill Clinton, who campaigned for him in the race's final days, the Mississippi Clarion Ledger, part of the USA TODAY Network, reported.

The contest attracted national attention as outside groups and party organizations poured millions of dollars into Mississippi, sensing an opportunity in a state Republicans had comfortably carried for decades.

The outcome was historic on multiple fronts. Colom became the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since 1982 and the first Black Mississippian elected to the Senate since the Reconstruction era.

His victory over Hyde-Smith, who had served in the Senate since 2018, was widely described by national political observers as one of the biggest surprises of the 2026 midterm elections and immediately fueled discussion about whether the result could signal broader shifts in Southern politics.

Bill Clinton: Blue Mississippi sure has a nice ring to it

Clinton celebrated the outcome on X.

"We may have had to count One Mississippi, Two Mississippi, but Blue Mississippi sure has a nice ring to it! Scott, you put your heart and soul into this race because you believe in the promise of your state's people. And they believed in you right back. I'm honored to have stood alongside you. Congratulations!"

The message echoed a broader sentiment among national Democrats who portrayed the result as evidence that Democrats can compete in states long considered safely Republican.

Chuck Schumer: 'Blue Mississippi Is Here'

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer quickly hailed the result, posting on X:

"Blue Mississippi is here. Scott Colom is the only person who could've gotten this done. I knew it from the moment I met him."

Schumer's comments reflected the surprise and excitement among Democratic leaders after a victory few national analysts predicted when the campaign began.

Cory Booker highlights historic nature of win

For many Democrats, the election carried significance beyond party politics.

U.S. Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey emphasized Colom's place in history.

"Congratulations to my friend, Senator-elect Scott Colom. History was made today. You showed that hope rises in the South, and that Mississippi matters!"

Booker's remarks echoed a theme repeated throughout the day by Democratic officials and civil-rights advocates who pointed to Colom becoming Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

Bernie Sanders praises progressive message

U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont focused on the substance of Colom's campaign, arguing voters responded to an anti-establishment economic message.

"Congratulations to Scott Colom on winning his election and making history as Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction.

Scott ran on a bold agenda — taking on Big Tech, the billionaire class and corruption in Washington — and WON.

Scott: Welcome to the Senate."

Sanders' endorsement of Colom's message added a progressive dimension to the national reaction surrounding the race.

Amy Klobuchar focuses on senate flip

U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota highlighted the electoral implications of the victory.

"Congratulations to Scott Colom on flipping Mississippi's Senate seat blue for the first time in nearly 40 years! What a great senator he will be!"

Her comments underscored how Democrats viewed the Mississippi result not simply as an individual victory but as the capture of a Senate seat that had been in Republican hands for decades.

Kamala Harris weighs in historic night

Former Vice President Kamala Harris, who campaigned with Colom during the race, also celebrated the victory on X, writing that "the power is with the people, and the people of Mississippi are with Scott."

Harris called Colom's election "history" in the making, noting that he would become Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction. She added that she had seen firsthand while campaigning with him in his hometown that he is "a brilliant leader," and said Mississippi voters had chosen a candidate who will fight for their future.

Mississippi Democrats join celebration

Reaction also poured in from Mississippi Democrats.

Former gubernatorial nominee Brandon Presley wrote:

"It is official, Mississippi has a new voice in Washington and it is Senator-Elect Scott Colom. Katelyn and I couldn't be happier for this beautiful family and our beloved Mississippi."

Gov. Tate Reeves wants to work with Colom

Even as national Democrats celebrated the upset, Gov. Tate Reeves struck a bipartisan tone in his public response. The Republican governor congratulated Scott Colom in a post on X and signaled a willingness to work with the senator-elect despite their political differences.

"Congratulations to Senator-Elect Scott Colom," Reeves wrote. "I hope to collaborate as we continue our very important work to support Mississippi families, grow jobs and wages for our people, and improve educational outcomes for our kids."

Reeves' message reflected an emphasis on cooperation and governing priorities as Mississippi prepares to send a new senator to Washington.

Cindy Hyde-Smith Concedes

The outpouring of reaction came after Hyde-Smith formally conceded defeat, bringing an end to one of the nation's closest and most closely watched Senate races.

In a video posted to social media, Hyde-Smith said she accepted the outcome and congratulated her opponent.

"While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state."

A result that resonated beyond Mississippi

The wave of reaction illustrated how quickly the race became a national political story. Democratic leaders celebrated a victory in a state President Trump carried comfortably two years earlier, while many focused on the historical significance of electing Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction and its first Democratic senator since 1982. National media outlets widely characterized the result as one of the biggest surprises of the 2026 midterm election cycle.

 is a writer for the Clarion Ledger, part of the USA TODAY Network. He can be reached at rreily@gannett.com. You can follow him on the X platform, formerly known as Twitter @GreenOkra1.

news.title: Another GOP defeat: Mississippi elects first Black senator since 1874
news.text: More than a week after the U.S. midterm elections delivered sweeping Democratic gains and cost Republicans control of both houses of Congress, Democrat Scott Colom has completed another extraordinary upset, defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi. The victory gives Democrats their 55th Senate seat, compared with 44 for Republicans, with only the race in Alaska still unresolved. The result is particularly striking in Mississippi, one of the most reliably conservative states in the country. Democrats also scored breakthroughs in traditionally Republican territory elsewhere in the midterms, but Colom’s victory carries a distinction of its own: He is the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since John Stennis won reelection in 1982. Colom, 43, defeated Hyde-Smith, 67, who had served in the Senate since 2018. President Donald Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election. Colom also becomes Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since the Reconstruction era following the Civil War. Mississippi sent two Black Republicans to the Senate during Reconstruction: Hiram Revels, who served in 1870 and 1871, and Blanche K. Bruce, who was born into slavery and was elected by the Mississippi Legislature in 1874 before serving a full Senate term from 1875 to 1881. The historical significance of Colom’s victory is amplified by Mississippi’s subsequent history of racial segregation and Black disenfranchisement under Jim Crow. During Reconstruction, the Ku Klux Klan also emerged as a violent white supremacist organization targeting Black Americans and their political rights. Among the symbolic results this year was Colom’s victory in Forrest County, a traditionally Republican county named for Confederate Gen. Nathan Bedford Forrest, the Klan’s first grand wizard. The Mississippi race remained undecided for more than a week as election officials processed absentee and provisional ballots. Colom finished election night with a lead of just 43 votes, but his advantage steadily expanded as counties completed their counts. The Associated Press called the race after his lead grew to more than 4,600 votes, a margin large enough that the remaining ballots were not expected to change the outcome. Hyde-Smith subsequently conceded. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer celebrated the result on X. “Blue Mississippi is here. Scott Colom is the only person who could’ve gotten this done. I knew it from the moment I met him,” he wrote. “Scott will make a fantastic Senator for the people of Mississippi, and I can’t wait to welcome him to the Senate.” The only Senate contest still outstanding is Alaska. Democrats already hold a 55-44 advantage in the incoming 100-member Senate. A victory in Alaska would increase that majority to 56 seats, significant because most legislation subject to a filibuster requires 60 votes to end debate. The closer Democrats move to that threshold, the fewer Republican votes they would need to advance such measures. The upset forecasters missed and the protein ad behind it Unlike races in some other Republican strongholds that had attracted attention well before Election Day, Mississippi was not initially expected to become one of the country’s closest Senate contests. There were signs that Hyde-Smith was vulnerable and that voters were frustrated over the cost of living and high fuel prices, but the Cook Political Report rated the race “Solid Republican” until late October before shifting it to “Likely Republican.” Trump’s commanding 2024 performance reinforced those assumptions. But Colom spent months insisting that the political environment in Mississippi was changing and urging national Democrats to invest more heavily in his campaign. He argued that unusually strong Black turnout, combined with dissatisfaction over prices and the Trump administration, could make the race competitive. Black residents make up roughly 37% of Mississippi’s population. The morning after Election Day, while much of the country was still surprised by the razor-thin result, Colom said his campaign had expected exactly that kind of race. “Unlike all the people across the country that might be surprised, our campaign, our volunteers, the people of Mississippi are not surprised,” he said. His team had prepared lawyers and volunteers across the state to monitor the remaining count. Colom’s fundraising accelerated late in the campaign, and prominent Democrats including former Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Bill Clinton traveled to Mississippi to support him. But much of his campaign remained intensely local, centered on town halls, grassroots organizing and appeals to voters who had traditionally supported Republicans. His central themes were the cost of living, health care and high gasoline and grocery prices. Hyde-Smith inadvertently provided Colom with one of his most effective campaign messages. Asked in a local television interview about rising beef prices, she responded, “You have so many proteins to choose from.” Colom’s campaign turned the remark into a viral advertisement featuring Mississippi voters reacting incredulously to the suggestion. One man grilling hamburgers told the camera: “Pick another protein? I’d rather pick another senator instead.” The ad drew millions of views and became shorthand for Colom’s argument that Hyde-Smith was disconnected from the economic pressures facing ordinary residents. He continued the joke on the campaign trail, including appearances involving food trucks offering voters different protein choices. Colom is a seventh-generation Mississippian, a father of two and a practicing Christian who made his faith and family history central parts of his campaign. His mother, Dorothy Colom, broke racial barriers when she was elected a chancery court judge, while his father, Wilbur Colom, was a prominent attorney and longtime Republican who worked for Ronald Reagan. Before running for the Senate, Colom had already made history in Mississippi politics. He served as a judge and prosecutor before winning election in 2015 as district attorney for the state’s 16th Judicial District, becoming the first Black person elected to the post. He built his Senate campaign around the argument that he could attract both the state’s large Black electorate and moderate or traditionally Republican voters. His victory now places him in a political lineage stretching directly back to Reconstruction. Colom has said the significance of becoming Mississippi’s first Black senator in generations also carries a responsibility to ensure that he is not the last, and that his performance in office should make it easier rather than harder for future candidates from similar backgrounds to succeed. The election also carries an element of personal political reversal. President Joe Biden nominated Colom in 2022 to become a federal judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Republican Sen. Roger Wicker supported the nomination, but Hyde-Smith refused to return the Senate Judiciary Committee’s required “blue slip,” preventing it from advancing. Hyde-Smith later boasted about blocking the nomination. “He thought he was going to be a federal judge, and I blocked him,” she said during her reelection campaign. Colom has denied that his Senate run was motivated by revenge, instead emphasizing affordability, health care and government accountability. Now, the man Hyde-Smith prevented from reaching the federal bench will replace her in the U.S. Senate. As Colom put it while the ballots were still being counted: “The bottom line is this is the beginning of a new direction for our state.”
news.summary: Nine days after Democrats seized both chambers of Congress, Scott Colom ousts Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in deep-red Mississippi, becoming the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and giving Democrats their 55th Senate seat

news.title: How Scott Colom won Mississippi’s Senate race
news.text:
In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom has defeated Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. By many metrics, Colom’s victory is nothing short of remarkable: Mississippi was the “reddest” of Democrats’ Senate pickups this year, a state President Donald Trump carried by 23 points in 2024.

So how did Colom do it? He won with an electorate that looked different from 2024’s, a small but decisive slice of Trump voters and Mississippians who wanted a check on the president.

Colom’s raw vote total has exceeded Kamala Harris’ 2024 total — an impressive feat, given that midterms draw far fewer voters than presidential elections. With 99% of votes counted, Colom has received roughly 473,000 votes, already several thousand more than Harris’ roughly 467,000. At the same time, Hyde-Smith earned nearly 300,000 fewer votes than Trump won in the state two years ago.

Colom’s relative strength was not limited to any one place. He won 38 of Mississippi’s 82 counties, including 18 that Trump carried in 2024. Ten of those were counties Democrats also lost in 2020.

Colom didn’t just win parts of the state that backed Trump heavily — he did so decisively. He carried 10 counties by double digits that Trump carried in 2024. In Forrest County, named after the first Grand Wizard of the Ku Klux Klan, Colom won by more than 10 points. In Lowndes and Pike, both Trump 2024 counties, his margins were 16 and 18 points, respectively. Even where Colom trailed Hyde-Smith, his vote totals often approached or exceeded Harris’ in 2024. That held Hyde-Smith to single-digit margins in counties like Wayne and Lauderdale, which Trump carried by double digits.

A different electorate

The Voter Poll suggests that, measured by past vote, Mississippi’s 2026 electorate remained quite Republican, but that turnout patterns shifted it to the left. Trump won Mississippi 61%-38% in 2024. This year’s voters told us they supported him 54%-42% in 2024, about half his actual margin. These numbers are estimates but suggest that hundreds of thousands of Trump voters in Mississippi didn’t cast a Senate vote and that Harris voters were much likelier to turn out this year.

Turnout was especially high in majority-Black counties, which Colom won overwhelmingly. There, turnout was roughly 88% of 2024 presidential levels, compared with 75% in all other counties.

But even as Colom’s raw vote performance rivaled Democratic presidential totals, turnout alone likely does not account for his margin of victory. Data from the MS NOW Voter Poll suggests that voters distinguished Colom from the Democratic Party overall. They also saw him as a potential check on the Trump administration.

The Trump crossover

In addition to strong turnout, Colom needed some crossover support to win — and that is exactly what he got. He retained nearly all (99%) of Harris’ voters who turned out this year. By contrast, just 88% of Trump voters supported Hyde-Smith, while 8% picked Colom, according to The Voter Poll. That may seem like a small crossover rate but it was enough to be decisive.

Colom also won voters with annual family incomes under $50,000, a group that made up a plurality of Senate voters in the state. Hyde-Smith won those in the next-highest income category, $50,000 to $100,000.

The Voter Poll data also suggests Colom’s electoral success stems in part from his ability to distance himself from his party. Views of both parties are underwater in Mississippi, but more voters hold unfavorable views of the Democratic Party (58%) than the Republican Party (52%). Yet Colom won 15% of those with an unfavorable view of his party, as well as 6% of Republicans.

Winning on the economy

Colom also performed well on the issue on which Mississippi voters express greater skepticism toward Democrats: the economy. The GOP holds an 11-point advantage over the Democratic Party on which party is better able to handle the economy (47% to 36%). But even as 42% of voters noted the economy as the most important issue facing the country today, most of these voters supported Colom over Hyde-Smith. And Colom’s vote share grew among voters expressing greater concern about the cost of gas and groceries.

A check on Trump

Finally, Colom benefited from backlash to the Trump administration, even in deep-red Mississippi. A majority of the state’s midterm voters disapprove of Trump, and nearly half strongly disapprove. Ninety-six percent of those strong disapprovers backed Colom. Most Mississippi voters also feel Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S. About two-thirds said Congress is not doing enough to provide checks and balances on the presidency, and those voters broke for Colom, 72% to 26%.

There’s also evidence of late momentum for Colom. Voters who decided whom to back in the last month broke for Colom by 15 points, while those who decided earlier were more likely to pick Hyde-Smith.

Taken together, the numbers point to a candidate who benefited from favorable turnout but didn’t rely on that alone. In a state Trump carried by 23 points two years ago, Colom needed a changed electorate, a sliver of Trump voters and backlash against the president. He got all three.
